arXiv:2511.03353v1 [math.MG] 05 Nov 2025
The hexagonal lattice is universally locally optimal
Thomas Leblé
††thanks: Université de Paris-Cité, CNRS, MAP5 UMR 8145, F-75006 Paris, France thomas.leble@math.cnrs.fr
August 24, 2026
Abstract
We prove that the hexagonal lattice is a local minimizer, among all point configurations, of the interaction energy per unit volume for pair potentials that are completely monotonic functions of the square distance. This includes Gaussian interactions and power laws.
Dedicated to Sylvia Serfaty on the occasion of her 50^{th} birthday.
1 Introduction
When f:(0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R} is a function, and \mathsf{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is a locally finite collection of points, define the f-energy
\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{X}):=\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|\mathsf{X}\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\sum_{x,y\in\mathsf{X}\cap\mathrm{B}_{r},x\neq y}f(|x-y|),
(1.1)
where \mathrm{B}_{r} is the disk of center 0 and radius r, while |\mathsf{X}\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}| is the number of points in \mathrm{B}_{r}.
The goal of this paper is to prove that if f is of the form f:r\mapsto e^{-\pi\alpha r^{2}}, or f:r\mapsto r^{-s}, then the hexagonal lattice \mathsf{A}_{2} is a local minimizer of \mathrm{E}_{f} among point configurations. Our result extends to all completely monotonic functions of the square distance, see Section 1.2.
An important conjecture states that \mathsf{A}_{2} is in fact the global minimizer of those energies at fixed density. However, we are not aware of any local minimality result.
1.1 The hexagonal lattice
We denote by \mathsf{A}_{2} the hexagonal lattice \mathsf{A}_{2}:=\sigma\mathbb{Z}+\tau\mathbb{Z}, seen as a collection of points in \mathbb{R}^{2}, where:
\sigma:=r_{\star}\times(1,0),\quad\tau:=r_{\star}\times\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right),\quad r_{\star}:=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}}.
The quantity r_{\star} is the minimal distance between lattice points. A fundamental domain \mathcal{H} of \mathsf{A}_{2} is given by the Voronoi cell of the origin, i.e. the set of points which are closer to the origin than to any other lattice point, see Figure 1. With our choice of r_{\star}, the area of \mathcal{H} (the “covolume”) is equal to 1.
\mathcal{H}\sigma\tau
Figure 1: The hexagonal lattice \mathsf{A}_{2}, its basis (\sigma,\tau), and the fundamental domain \mathcal{H}.
In this paper, “local” is understood with respect to small, bounded perturbations of the lattice: take \mathbf{p}:\mathsf{A}_{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}, and consider the perturbed lattice obtained by shifting each lattice point x by \mathbf{p}(x):
\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}:=\{x+\mathbf{p}(x),\ x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\}.
We define the size of a perturbation \mathbf{p} as
\|\mathbf{p}\|:=\sup_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}|\mathbf{p}(x)|.
Whenever \|\mathbf{p}\| is finite, the resulting point configuration \mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p} has density 1, in the sense that
\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\left|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}\right|=1.
(1.2)
In order to ensure that \mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p} remains simple, and to shorten some computations, we assume that:
\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{1}{20}r_{\star}.
(1.3)
Since we are aiming at local results, this is not restrictive. We often write \mathbf{p}_{x} instead of \mathbf{p}(x).
1.2 Main results
For \alpha>0, denote by \Phi_{\alpha} the Gaussian interaction potential \Phi_{\alpha}:r\mapsto e^{-\pi\alpha r^{2}}. Our first result is:
Theorem 1.
For all \alpha>0, there exists \varepsilon (depending on \alpha) such that:
If \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon, then \mathrm{E}_{\Phi_{\alpha}}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\geq\mathrm{E}_{\Phi_{\alpha}}(\mathsf{A}_{2}).
(1.4)
The value of \varepsilon can be chosen uniformly for \alpha in compact subsets of (0,+\infty).
Following [CK07], there is a strong interest in considering more general interaction potentials f that are completely monotonic functions of square distance (we call them here “c.m.s.d”). Recall that a smooth function g is completely monotonic when (-1)^{k}g^{(k)}\geq 0 for all k\geq 0. A c.m.s.d function is then defined as being of the form f(r)=g(r^{2}), where g is completely monotonic. It follows from a theorem of Bernstein that every c.m.s.d function f can be written as a mixture of Gaussians, i.e. there exists a certain positive measure \mathrm{W}_{f} on [0,+\infty) such that for all r>0, the following integral is finite and:
\int_{0}^{+\infty}\Phi_{\alpha}(r)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)=f(r).
(1.5)
Theorem 2.
Let f be a c.m.s.d function. There exists \varepsilon>0 (depending on f) such that:
If \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon, then \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\geq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}).
(1.6)
More generally, let \mathcal{F} be a family of c.m.s.d. functions, and assume that the following condition is satisfied:
\lim_{\alpha_{0}\to 0,\alpha_{1}\to\infty}\frac{\displaystyle{\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}\alpha^{-1}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)}}{\displaystyle{\int_{1}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{1}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)}}=0\text{ uniformly for $f\in\mathcal{F}$.}
(1.7)
Then \mathsf{A}_{2} is uniformly locally optimal for f\in\mathcal{F}, namely there exists \varepsilon>0 such that:
If \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon, then \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\geq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) for all f\in\mathcal{F}.
Remark 1.1.
When writing (1.6), we implicitly assume \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2})<+\infty, which, for a c.m.s.d function f, is equivalent to r\mapsto rf(r) being integrable at infinity, or to \alpha\mapsto\alpha^{-1} being \mathrm{W}_{f}-integrable at 0, see (3.53). Otherwise, it is easy to see that both sides of (1.6) are +\infty.
The power-law (or Riesz) potentials f_{s}:r\to r^{-s} are c.m.s.d functions whose measure \mathrm{W}_{s} has density:
\frac{\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{s}}{\mathtt{d}\alpha}=\frac{\pi^{\frac{s}{2}}\alpha^{\frac{s}{2}-1}}{\Gamma(\frac{s}{2})}.
(1.8)
As a direct application of Theorem 2, we obtain that \mathsf{A}_{2} is locally optimal for every f_{s}, and that \varepsilon can be chosen uniformly for s in compact subsets of (2,+\infty) (when s\leq 2, the interaction energies are infinite).
1.3 Connection with the literature and the “universal optimality” conjecture
The lattice \mathsf{A}_{2} is famously optimal with respect to circle packing. It is moreover known, or expected, to solve many other optimization problems, see [Gru00]. This is an instance of “crystallization”, namely the observation that, in various settings, optimal point configurations exhibit a regular structure, see [BL15].
In that regard, a major open problem consists in proving that \mathsf{A}_{2} is “universally optimal” for energy minimization, i.e. is a global minimizer, among point configurations of density 1 in the sense of (1.2), of every Gaussian interaction energy, see [CK07, Conjecture 9.4] - such interactions are sometimes referred to as the Gaussian core model in the physics literature [Sti76]. By Bernstein’s theorem, this would imply global minimality for every c.m.s.d interaction potential. Partial results are few:
•
In [Mon88], Montgomery proved that \mathsf{A}_{2} minimizes all those energies among lattices. This result has later been generalized in many directions, see e.g. [SS12, Theorem 2] for an extension to the Coulomb energy, or [BF23] and references therein for variations on the topic of minimization among lattices.
•
Some recent results have gone slightly beyond the lattice case, for instance [HT25] shows universal optimality of \mathsf{A}_{2} among point configurations with a period of 4 or 6 points.
•
A proof of local optimality among all periodic configurations - with an implicit dependency on the period - had been given in [CS12], but a flaw was unfortunately later found by the authors [CS22].
•
As put in [FSZ24] “the status of universal optimality of the hexagonal lattice has been set back to the result of Montgomery from 1988”.
In this paper, we prove local minimality of \mathsf{A}_{2} for all c.m.s.d functions, together with a quantitative understanding, in terms of f, of:
1.
The size \varepsilon of the neighborhood around \mathsf{A}_{2} on which we guarantee local minimality of \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}).
2.
A lower bound, in terms of \mathbf{p}, on \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) when \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon.
Moreover, we obtain a form of “local universal optimality”, as we show that \varepsilon can be chosen uniformly for reasonable families of c.m.s.d functions, see Theorem 2. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first results of this kind. However, it is fair to say that:
•
We remain far from the full conjecture, both qualitatively and quantitatively (our \varepsilon’s are very small).
•
The techniques are local by nature and cannot possibly yield a global result.
Remark 1.2.
In dimension 8 and 24, both sphere packing and universal optimality were recently solved thanks to major breakthroughs by Viazovska et al. We refer to [CKM+22, Sec. 1] for an introduction to such problems and a survey of what is known, or expected, in other dimensions.
1.4 Plan of the paper
Since c.m.s.d functions are mixtures of the \Phi_{\alpha}’s, most of the work is devoted to proving, in a quantitative way, that \mathsf{A}_{2} is locally optimal with respect to Gaussian interactions.
•
In Section 2, we introduce some important tools and lemmas. In particular:
–
We show that it is enough to consider periodic perturbations (Lemma 2.1).
–
We present a “periodic” version of the 2-design property for regular hexagons (Proposition 2.9).
–
We state a key minimality result for a certain lattice sum (Proposition 2.12).
•
In Section 3, we prove a quantitative version of Theorem 1, then use it to deduce Theorem 2.
•
An appendix is devoted to the proof of auxiliary results. In particular, Appendix C, which takes up a significant portion of the paper, consists in proving the minimality result of Proposition 2.12.
Acknowledgements. We thank Sylvia Serfaty for introducing us to such topics quite some time ago. We thank Martin Huesmann for initial discussions, and Antoine Tilloy for his help with positivity questions.
2 Preliminaries
We denote the inner product of two vectors x,y of \mathbb{R}^{2} by x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}y.
2.1 Convention for Fourier analysis on \mathbb{R}^{2}
Fourier transforms.
We define the Fourier transform \hat{\varphi} of a Schwartz function \varphi as:
\hat{\varphi}:k\mapsto\hat{\varphi}(k):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\varphi(x)e^{-2i\pi x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}\mathtt{d}x.
With this convention, the Gaussian11
1
\mathsf{G}_{\alpha} is a function \mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} whereas in Section 1.2, the function \Phi_{\alpha} is [0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}. We have \mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)=\Phi_{\alpha}(|x|). family \mathsf{G}_{\alpha}:x\mapsto e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}} on \mathbb{R}^{2} satisfies
\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}=\alpha^{-1}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha^{-1}}\text{ for $\alpha>0$.}
(2.1)
Reciprocal lattice and Pontryagin dual.
We denote by \widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} the reciprocal lattice of \mathsf{A}_{2}, defined as:
\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}:=\left\{k\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\ k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}x\in\mathbb{Z}\text{ for all }x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\right\}.
In practice \widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} corresponds to applying a rotation of angle \frac{\pi}{2} to \mathsf{A}_{2}. We denote by \Omega the fundamental domain of \widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} obtained by applying the same rotation to \mathcal{H}.
The Pontryagin dual of \mathsf{A}_{2} is the torus \mathbb{R}^{2}/\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}, which can be identified with \Omega.
Poisson summation formula.
If \varphi:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} is a Schwartz function and u\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, we have:
\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}\varphi(x+u)=\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}\hat{\varphi}(k)e^{2i\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u}.
2.2 Periodic functions and Fourier transforms.
We will use sub-lattices of the form N\mathsf{A}_{2}:=N\sigma\mathbb{Z}+N\tau\mathbb{Z} for some integer N\geq 1, where \sigma,\tau are the basis vectors of \mathsf{A}_{2}. The reciprocal lattice of N\mathsf{A}_{2} is given by
\widehat{N\mathsf{A}_{2}}=\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}.
We say that a function g defined on \mathsf{A}_{2} is N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic if
g(x+y)=g(x)\text{ for all $x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}$ and all $y\in N\mathsf{A}_{2}$}.
(2.2)
Equivalently22
2
We will abuse notation and not distinguish between g and the corresponding map on the quotient space., g can be seen as function on the discrete torus \mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}. When g is N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic, we define its Fourier transform as the following function, defined for “frequencies” k in \frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}:
\hat{g}:=k\mapsto\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}g(x^{\prime})e^{-2i\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}x^{\prime}}.
(2.3)
Then the Plancherel identity holds:
\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}|g(x^{\prime})|^{2}=\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}|\hat{g}(k)|^{2}.
(2.4)
We refer e.g. to the lecture notes [Tao07] for a pedagogical presentation of this topic.
2.3 Reduction to periodic perturbations
Lemma 2.1.
Let f be a c.m.s.d function. Let \mathbf{p} be a perturbation such that \|\mathbf{p}\|<+\infty, and let \delta>0. There exists N\geq 1 and a perturbation \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}} which is N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic in the sense of (2.2), such that:
1.
The size of perturbations does not increase: \|\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}}\|\leq\|\mathbf{p}\|.
2.
The corresponding f-energy increases by at most \delta:
\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\leq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})+\delta.
The proof of Lemma 2.1 is elementary, we postpone it to Section A. In order to prove local minimality results, it is thus enough to study periodic perturbations - provided that our analysis does not depend on the size of the period.
2.4 Properties of periodic perturbations
Let \mathsf{L} be a sub-lattice of \mathsf{A}_{2}, let \mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L} be the quotient set, which is finite, and let \mathbf{p} be a \mathsf{L}-periodic perturbation. For x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}, we define \mathrm{Q}_{x} as the following probability measure on \mathbb{R}^{2}:
\mathrm{Q}_{x}:=\frac{1}{|\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}|}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}}\delta_{\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}+x}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}}.
(2.5)
This object is crucial for us. It encodes the distribution of “relative displacements” in the direction x.
Remark 2.2.
Since x^{\prime}\mapsto x^{\prime}+x\mod\mathsf{L} is a permutation of \mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}, the measure \mathrm{Q}_{x} is always centered:
\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}}\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}+x}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}=0.
Energy of \mathsf{A}_{2} plus periodic perturbations.
For \alpha>0, denote by \mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{X}) the \Phi_{\alpha}-energy of a point configuration \mathsf{X} in the sense of (1.1).
Lemma 2.3.
If \mathbf{p} is a periodic perturbation, we have:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},x\neq 0}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\Phi_{\alpha}\left(|x+u|\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u).
(2.6)
In particular,
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},x\neq 0}\Phi_{\alpha}\left(|x|\right).
Proof.
This is essentially [CK07, Lemma 9.1], which states33
3
Their \Lambda is our \mathsf{L}, their N is our |\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}|, and their points v corresponds to our perturbed lattice points x+\mathbf{p}_{x}. Their sum runs over x\in\mathsf{L} such that x+x^{\prime}-x^{\prime\prime}+\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime\prime}}\neq 0. Since we work under the assumption (1.3), and \mathbf{p} is \mathsf{L}-periodic, we have x+x^{\prime}-x^{\prime\prime}+\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime\prime}}=0 iff x+x^{\prime}-x^{\prime\prime}=0:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})=\frac{1}{|\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}|}\sum_{x^{\prime},x^{\prime\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}}\ \sum_{x\in\mathsf{L},x+x^{\prime}-x^{\prime\prime}\neq 0}\Phi_{\alpha}\left(|x+x^{\prime}+\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}-x^{\prime\prime}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime\prime}}|\right).
Since \mathbf{p} is \mathsf{L}-periodic we may replace \mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}} by \mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}+x}. Moreover, when x^{\prime} varies in \mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L} and x varies in \mathsf{L}, then x^{\prime\prime\prime}:=x+x^{\prime} varies in \mathsf{A}_{2}. We thus have:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})=\frac{1}{|\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}|}\sum_{x^{\prime\prime\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}\ \sum_{x^{\prime\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L},x^{\prime\prime\prime}-x^{\prime\prime}\neq 0}\Phi_{\alpha}\left(|x^{\prime\prime\prime}-x^{\prime\prime}+\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime\prime\prime}}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime\prime}}|\right).
For x^{\prime\prime} in \mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}, when x^{\prime\prime\prime} varies in \mathsf{A}_{2}\setminus\{x^{\prime\prime}\}, then y:=x^{\prime\prime\prime}-x^{\prime\prime} varies in \mathsf{A}_{2}\setminus\{0\}. We may thus write:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})=\sum_{y\in\mathsf{A}_{2},y\neq 0}\left(\frac{1}{|\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}|}\sum_{x^{\prime\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}}\Phi_{\alpha}\left(|y+\mathbf{p}_{y+x^{\prime\prime}}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime\prime}}|\right)\right),
and by definition of \mathrm{Q}_{x}, the right-hand side coincides with the right-hand side of (2.6).
∎
Probabilistic formulation.
If \mathbf{p} is \mathsf{L}-periodic for some sub-lattice \mathsf{L}, let \mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}} be the random family of vectors defined by:
\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}:=(\mathbf{p}_{x+x^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}})_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}},
(2.7)
where x^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}} is chosen uniformly at random in the period \mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}. It is \mathsf{A}_{2}-stationary in the sense that:
For all z\in\mathsf{A}_{2}, \left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}\right)_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}} and \left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x+z}\right)_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}} have the same finite-dimensional distributions.
(2.8)
With this point of view, the measure \mathrm{Q}_{x} defined in (2.5) represents the law of \mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}. In particular:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)=\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}\right|^{2}\right].
(2.9)
2.5 The autocorrelation function
Let \mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}} be a random, \mathsf{A}_{2}-stationary perturbation in the sense of (2.8). For x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}, let \mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{x},\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{x} be the coordinates of \mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x} in the canonical basis. Assume that \mathbb{E}\left[\left|\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}\right|^{2}\right] is finite.
•
We define \mathrm{C}:\mathsf{A}_{2}\to\mathcal{M}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) as:
\mathrm{C}:x\mapsto\left(\begin{matrix}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{0}\right)^{2}\right]&\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{0}\right)\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{0}\right)\right]\\
\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{0}\right)\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{0}\right)\right]&\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{0}\right)^{2}\right]\end{matrix}\right).
(2.10)
We write \mathrm{C}_{x} for the value of the matrix at x\in\mathsf{A}_{2} and denote by \mathrm{C}^{ab}_{x} (a,b\in\{1,2\}) its coefficients.
•
We define the autocorrelation \mathrm{R}:\mathsf{A}_{2}\to\mathcal{M}_{2}(\mathbb{R})
\mathrm{R}:x\mapsto\left(\begin{matrix}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{x}\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{0}\right]&\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{x}\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{0}+\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{x}\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{0}\right)\right]\\
\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{x}\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{0}+\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{x}\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(1)}_{0}\right)\right]&\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{x}\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}(2)}_{0}\right]\end{matrix}\right),
(2.11)
We write similarly \mathrm{R}_{x} and \mathrm{R}^{ab}_{x} for a,b\in\{1,2\}.
Denote by T the transpose of a matrix. We have, for all x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}:
\mathrm{C}_{x}=\mathbb{E}\left[(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0})(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0})^{T}\right],\quad\mathrm{R}_{x}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0})^{T}+\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x})^{T}\right].
Using stationarity, a direct computation gives:
\mathrm{C}_{x}=2\left(\mathrm{R}_{0}-\mathrm{R}_{x}\right),\quad\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}\right)^{2}\right]=\mathtt{tr}\mathrm{C}_{x}=2\mathtt{tr}\left(\mathrm{R}_{0}-\mathrm{R}_{x}\right).
(2.12)
Observe that \mathrm{R} is a positive semidefinite matrix-valued function in the following sense: for all maps h:\mathsf{A}_{2}\to\mathbb{C} with finite support, the matrix
\sum_{x,y\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}h(x)\overline{h(y)}\mathrm{R}_{x-y}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}h(x)\overline{h(y)}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{y})^{T}+\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{y}(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x})^{T}\right]
is positive semi-definite. This has important “spectral” consequences, as we present next.
2.6 Spectral measure(s)
Denote by \mathsf{S}_{2}^{+} the cone of symmetric positive 2\times 2 matrices with real coefficients. A \mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}-valued measure is a map defined on the Borel \sigma-algebra of \mathbb{R}^{2}, with values in \mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}, satisfying the natural requirements (\sigma-additivity etc.) for being a measure, see [Kim11, Sec. 1.2 & 1.3].
Existence of the spectral measure.
The following result generalizes Bochner’s theorem on Fourier transforms of positive-definite functions.
Lemma 2.4 ([Fal69]).
There exists a \mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}-valued measure \widehat{\mathsf{R}}, defined on the Pontryagin dual \Omega, such that:
\mathrm{R}_{x}=\int_{\Omega}\cos\left(2\pi x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\omega\right)\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\text{ for all }x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}.
(2.13)
The measure \widehat{\mathsf{R}} is called the spectral measure of the perturbations. For a pedagogical presentation, building on the classical theorem of Bochner, we refer to [Kim11, Thm. 2.2.3]. We sketch the argument:
Proof.
Both x\mapsto\mathrm{R}^{11}_{x} and x\mapsto\mathrm{R}^{22}_{x} are positive-definite (real-valued) functions in the usual sense, so by Bochner’s theorem their Fourier transform is a finite positive measure on the Pontryagin dual \Omega. As for x\mapsto\mathrm{R}^{12}_{x}=\mathrm{R}^{21}_{x}, it is not positive-definite in general, but can easily be written as the difference of two positive-definite functions, thus its Fourier transform is a (signed) measure on \Omega, with finite total mass. It remains to check that those four measures put together define a \mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}-valued measure \widehat{\mathsf{R}}.
∎
Remark 2.5.
The general result is stated in the Hermitian case, however here \mathrm{R} is real-symmetric, and \mathrm{R}_{x}=\mathrm{R}_{-x} by stationarity, thus \mathrm{R}_{x}^{ab}=\int_{\Omega}\cos(2\pi x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\omega)\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}(\omega) and \mathrm{R}_{x}=\int_{\Omega}\cos(2\pi x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\omega)\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega).
The trace measure and trace derivative.
Let \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab} (a,b\in\{1,2\}) be the components of \widehat{\mathsf{R}}, which are (real-valued) finite measures on \Omega, corresponding to the Fourier transform of the components of \mathrm{R}. Define the (real-valued) “trace” measure \tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}} as:
\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}:=\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{11}+\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{22},
(2.14)
which is positive and finite, because so are \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{11} and \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{22}. Since \widehat{\mathsf{R}} takes values in \mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}, we know that for all a,b\in\{1,2\}, the measure \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab} is absolutely continuous with respect to \tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}. Define the “trace derivative” \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime} as the matrix-valued measurable map \omega\mapsto\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}(\omega), defined on \Omega, such that:
\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}:=\frac{\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}}{\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}}\text{ in the sense that }\left(\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}\right)^{ab}=\frac{\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}}{\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}}\text{ for $a,b\in\{1,2\}$.}
It follows from [Ros64] that for \tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}-a.e. \omega in \Omega, the matrix \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}(\omega) is in \mathsf{S}_{2}^{+} and can be diagonalized44
4
The choice of v_{1},v_{2},\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2} can be made in a measurable fashion [Wil72]. in some orthonormal basis (v_{1}(\omega),v_{2}(\omega)), with eigenvalues \lambda_{1}(\omega),\lambda_{2}(\omega) such that
\lambda_{1}(\omega)+\lambda_{2}(\omega)=1.
If f=(f_{1},f_{2}):\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{2} is bounded, we can write:
\sum_{a,b\in\{1,2\}}\int_{\Omega}f_{a}f_{b}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}=\int_{\Omega}\left(f\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}f\right)\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}=\int_{\Omega}\left(\lambda_{1}(f\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v_{1})^{2}+\lambda_{2}(f\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v_{2})^{2}\right)\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}.
(2.15)
Lemma 2.6.
We have for all x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\leq 8\pi^{2}|x|^{2}\mathtt{tr}\left(\int_{\Omega}|\omega|^{2}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\right).
Proof.
Using the definition of \widehat{\mathsf{R}} and the elementary inequality 1-\cos(\theta)\leq\theta^{2}, we have:
\mathrm{R}_{0}-\mathrm{R}_{x}=\int_{\Omega}\left(1-\cos(2\pi x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\omega)\right)\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\leq 4\pi^{2}\int_{\Omega}|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\omega|^{2}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\leq 4\pi^{2}|x|^{2}\int_{\Omega}|\omega|^{2}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega).
(2.16)
In particular, since taking 2\mathtt{tr}(\mathrm{R}_{0}-\mathrm{R}_{x}) yields the second moment of \mathrm{Q}_{x} (see (2.12) and (2.9)), we get:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)=2\mathtt{tr}(\mathrm{R}_{0}-\mathrm{R}_{x})\leq 8\pi^{2}|x|^{2}\mathtt{tr}\left(\int_{\Omega}|\omega|^{2}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\right).
(2.17)
∎
2.7 A “periodic 2-design” inequality
Regular hexagons are 2-designs.
Each non-zero lattice point is part of a “shell” of six distinct lattice points, obtained by applying a rotation of angle \frac{k\pi}{3} (k=0,\dots,5), which form the vertices of a regular hexagon. Regular hexagons enjoy a certain geometric property known as being a 2-design.
Definition 2.7.
[CS12, Lemma 4.3]
Let S be a finite set of points on the circle of radius r>0, assume that S is symmetric around the origin. It is said to be a spherical 2-design when for all u\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, we have:
\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{s\in S}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}r^{2}|u|^{2}.
(2.18)
The right-hand side of (2.18) is what one would obtain by averaging s\mapsto(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2} over the circle r\mathbb{S}^{1} of radius r, in other words we have the equality:
\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{s\in S}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}=\frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_{s\in r\mathbb{S}^{1}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}\mathtt{d}s.
(2.19)
Remark 2.8 (Regular hexagons are 5-designs).
For a regular hexagon of sidelength r, one can in fact replace the power 2 in (2.19) by any power up to 5. Equivalently (see [CS12, Definition 4.2 & Lemma 4.3]), for any polynomial \mathrm{P}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} of total degree up to 5, we have:
\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{s\in S}\mathrm{P}(s)=\frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_{s\in r\mathbb{S}^{1}}\mathrm{P}(s)\mathtt{d}s.
A periodic 2-design inequality.
If S is a “shell” of \mathsf{A}_{2} as described above, and (\mathrm{Q}_{x})_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}} are the measures associated to a periodic perturbation as in (2.5), can we ensure that, for some \mathtt{c}>0:
\sum_{s\in S}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{s}(u)\geq\mathtt{c}\sum_{s\in S}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{s}(u)\ ?
(2.20)
If we had \mathrm{Q}_{s}=\mathrm{Q} for some \mathrm{Q} independent on s, we could exchange the sum and the integral and write:
\sum_{s\in S}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{s}(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\sum_{s\in S}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}(u)=\frac{1}{2}r^{2}\times|S|\times\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}(u),
using the 2-design property (2.18), which would yield (2.20). The problem55
5
This is, in essence, one of the breaking points in [CS12], see their erratum [CS22]. is that \mathrm{Q}_{s} does depend on s.
The next proposition shows that, by averaging over a period, one recovers a certain inequality reminiscent of the 2-design property. For a regular hexagon, we sometimes say “radius” instead of sidelength.
Proposition 2.9 (Periodic 2-design inequality).
Let S be a shell of \mathsf{A}_{2} of radius r>0. Let \mathbf{p} be a perturbation which is N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic for some N\geq 1, in the sense of (2.2). We have:
\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}\left|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}(\mathbf{p}_{s+x^{\prime}}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}})\right|^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}r^{2}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}\left|\mathbf{p}_{s+x^{\prime}}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}\right|^{2}.
(2.21)
Using our definition (2.5) of the measures (\mathrm{Q}_{x})_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}, the inequality (2.21) (divided by N^{2}) yields (2.20) with \mathtt{c}=\frac{1}{4}r^{2}. The proof of Proposition 2.9 relies on the following geometric lemma:
Lemma 2.10.
Let S be the vertices of a regular hexagon of radius r, let k be in \mathbb{R}^{2}. For s\in S, define:
w_{s}(k):=2\left(1-\cos\left(2\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s\right)\right).
(2.22)
The following inequality holds for all v in \mathbb{R}^{2}:
\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}\left(\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)\right)r^{2}|v|^{2}.
(2.23)
We postpone the proof of Lemma 2.10 to Appendix B, and we explain how to deduce Proposition 2.9.
Proof of Proposition 2.9.
Let \mathbf{p} be a N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic perturbation and let \widehat{\mathbf{p}} be the Fourier transform of \mathbf{p} as in (2.3). We first fix s\in S and observe that for all frequencies k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}, we have
\widehat{\mathbf{p}_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}+s}}(k)=e^{-2i\pi s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k).
Dividing both sides of (2.21) by N^{2} and applying Plancherel’s identity (2.4) yields:
\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}\left|\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}+s}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}\right|^{2}=\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}}\left|e^{-2i\pi s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}-1\right|^{2}|\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k)|^{2},
(2.24)
as well as (using the fact that \widehat{s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\mathbf{p}}(k)=s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k) because the vector s is fixed):
\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}\left|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}(\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}+s}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}})\right|^{2}=\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}}\left|e^{-2i\pi s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}-1\right|^{2}|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k)|^{2}.
(2.25)
Define, as in (2.22), w_{s}(k):=\left|e^{-2i\pi s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}-1\right|^{2}=2\left(1-\cos\left(2\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s\right)\right). Inserting (2.24) and (2.25) into (2.21), the desired inequality becomes:
\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}}\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k)|^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}r^{2}\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}}\left(\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)\right)|\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k)|^{2}.
(2.26)
Then (2.26), and thus (2.21), follows from applying Lemma 2.10 for each frequency k.
∎
The constant \frac{1}{4} appears to be asymptotically sharp as N\to\infty.
Remark 2.11.
A square is also a spherical 2-design. However, the square lattice \mathbb{Z}^{2} - whoses shells are squares - does not satisfy (2.20) for any \mathtt{c}>0.
2.8 An auxiliary minimality lemma
Let v be a fixed unit vector in \mathbb{R}^{2}. For all \alpha>0, we consider the function \Psi_{\alpha}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to[0,+\infty) defined as:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}:u\mapsto\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}|(x+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|x+u|^{2}}
(2.27)
This function is clearly \mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic, so it is enough to study its restriction to the fundamental hexagon \mathcal{H}.
Proposition 2.12.
Let \alpha_{\dagger}>0 be fixed. There exists \mathtt{c}>0 such that for all \alpha\in(0,\alpha_{\dagger}) and for all u\in\mathcal{H}:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(2.28)
The proof of Proposition 2.12 relies on a cumbersome analysis given in Section C, including a handful of purely numerical inequalities. We emphasize that \Psi_{\alpha,v} is not convex. The value of \alpha_{\dagger} is irrelevant at this stage and will be chosen later, our argument works for all fixed \alpha_{\dagger} and becomes more difficult for small \alpha’s.
Remark 2.13.
In the sequel, we will encounter the function:
\omega\mapsto\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}|(k+\omega)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|k+\omega|^{2}}
where \omega lives in \Omega, the Pontryagin dual of \mathsf{A}_{2}. Since the reciprocal lattice \widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} is obtained from \mathsf{A}_{2} by a rotation and \Omega is obtained from \mathcal{H} by the same rotation, the conclusions of Proposition 2.12 apply readily.
3 Proof of Theorem 1
In this section, we denote by S^{\star} the first shell of \mathsf{A}_{2}, of sidelength r_{\star} (see Figure 1), and by \mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}) the “First-Shell” size of a perturbation \mathbf{p}, defined as (with \mathrm{Q}_{x} as in (2.5), see also (2.9)):
\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}):=\sum_{x\in S^{\star}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)
(3.1)
We also define, with \widehat{\mathsf{R}} the matrix-valued spectral measure of \mathbf{p} as introduced in Section 2.6:
\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}):=\mathtt{tr}\left(\int_{\Omega}|w|^{2}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\right).
(3.2)
By (2.17), if \mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p})=0 then \mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p})=0. Moreover if \mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p})=0, then clearly \mathbf{p} is constant. We prove the following quantitative version of Theorem 1:
Proposition 3.1.
There exists a threshold \alpha_{\dagger}>0 and a constant \mathtt{c}>0 such that the following holds.
Let \mathbf{p} be a periodic perturbation.
•
For \alpha\geq\alpha_{\dagger}, if \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\alpha^{-1}, then:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.3)
•
For 0<\alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger}, if \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}, then:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.4)
We divide the proof of Proposition 3.1 in two parts: “\alpha large” and “\alpha small”. The first case is easier, we simply use the periodic 2-design inequality of Section 2.7 to get a lower bound on the Hessian of the interaction energy. The second case is more subtle: it requires a distinction between “low” and “high” layers within \mathsf{A}_{2}, and the introduction of the spectral measure \widehat{\mathsf{R}} after having moved to Fourier side thanks to Poisson’s summation formula. The rest of this section is devoted to proving the following two lemmas.
Lemma 3.2 (Large \alpha).
There exists a threshold \alpha_{\dagger}\geq 1, a small constant \mathtt{c} and a large constant \mathtt{C} such that the following holds for all \alpha\geq\alpha_{\dagger} and all periodic perturbations \mathbf{p}:
•
If \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha}, we have:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.5)
•
Under our general assumption \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{20}, see (1.3), we have:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq-\mathtt{C}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.6)
Lemma 3.3 (Small \alpha).
With \alpha_{\dagger} as above, there exists a small constant \mathtt{c} and a large constant \mathtt{C} such that the following holds for all 0<\alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger} and all periodic perturbations \mathbf{p}:
•
If \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}, we have:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.7)
•
Under our general assumption \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{20}, see (1.3), we have:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq-\mathtt{C}\alpha^{-1}\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.8)
The lower bounds (3.6) and (3.8) are not needed for Proposition 3.1 but they follow from the same analysis and will be useful later when considering mixtures of the \Phi_{\alpha}’s in the proof of Theorem 2.
The starting point for both lemmas is (2.6), namely the fact that, with \mathrm{Q}_{x} as in (2.5):
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\setminus\{0\}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+u)-\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u),
(3.9)
where \mathsf{G}_{\alpha}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} is the Gaussian interaction potential \mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)=\Phi_{\alpha}(|x|)=e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}}.
3.1 First case: \alpha large
Without loss of generality, we can take here \alpha\geq 1. We start with the proof of (3.5) and assume that \mathbf{p} is bounded by \frac{1}{\alpha}.
Step 1. Taylor expansion.
In view of (3.9), for fixed x\in\mathsf{A}_{2} and u in \mathbb{R}^{2}, we use a second-order Taylor expansion:
\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+u)-\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)=\nabla\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u+\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+tu)(u,u)\mathtt{d}t,
and we integrate this identity against \mathrm{Q}_{x}. The first-order term vanishes thanks to Remark 2.2, and thus:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+u)-\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)=\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+tu)(u,u)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right)\mathtt{d}t.
(3.10)
For any z,u in \mathbb{R}^{2}, a direct computation gives:
\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(z)(u,u)=2\pi\alpha\left(2\pi\alpha\left|z\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\right|^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|z|^{2}}.
(3.11)
and then for t\in[0,1], applying (3.11) to z=x+tu yields:
\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+tu)\left(u,u\right)=2\pi\alpha\left(2\pi\alpha\left|(x+tu)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\right|^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|x+tu|^{2}},
(3.12)
Expanding the squares, using tx\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\geq-|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|, and discarding the non-negative 2\pi\alpha t^{2}|u|^{4} term, we get:
\left(2\pi\alpha\left|(x+tu)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\right|^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|x+tu|^{2}}\\
\geq\left(2\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|^{2}-4\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u||u|^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}-\pi\alpha t^{2}|u|^{2}-2\pi t\alpha x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u}.
(3.13)
Since we assume that \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha}, the measure \mathrm{Q}_{x} is supported on the disk \{u,|u|\leq\frac{2}{\alpha}\}. For |u|\leq\frac{2}{\alpha}, we have, for some \mathtt{C} independent of \alpha\geq 1 and of x,t,u:
4\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u||u|^{2}\leq\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|^{2}+\mathtt{C}|u|^{2}
(3.14)
using Young’s inequality first, then our assumption on |u|. For the same reasons:
0\leq\pi\alpha t^{2}|u|^{2}\leq\mathtt{C},\quad-\mathtt{C}|x|\leq 2\pi t\alpha x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\leq\mathtt{C}|x|.
(3.15)
Using (3.14), we get:
2\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|^{2}-4\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u||u|^{2}-|u|^{2}\geq\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|^{2}-(\mathtt{C}+1)|u|^{2},
and thus, returning to (3.13) and controlling the exponent by its worst/best value using (3.15):
\left(2\pi\alpha\left|(x+tu)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\right|^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|x+tu|^{2}}\geq\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}-\mathtt{C}|x|-\mathtt{C}}-(\mathtt{C}+1)|u|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+\mathtt{C}|x|}.
(3.16)
Step 2. A lower bound for the first shell.
We focus on the first shell of the lattice S^{\star}, of radius r_{\star}.
Claim 3.4.
There exists \mathtt{c}>0 such that, if \alpha is large enough:
\sum_{x\in S^{\star}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}-\mathtt{C}|x|-\mathtt{C}}-(\mathtt{C}+1)|u|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+\mathtt{C}|x|}\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\geq\mathtt{c}\alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.17)
Proof.
Using first Proposition 2.9, then the definition (3.1) of \mathsf{FS}, we have:
\sum_{x\in S^{\star}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}-\mathtt{C}|x|-\mathtt{C}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)=\pi\alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}-\mathtt{C}r_{\star}-\mathtt{C}}\times\left(\sum_{x\in S^{\star}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right)\\
\geq\pi\alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}-\mathtt{C}r_{\star}-\mathtt{C}}\times\frac{1}{4}\left(\sum_{x\in S^{\star}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right)=\left(\frac{\pi}{4}e^{-\mathtt{C}r_{\star}-\mathtt{C}}\right)\alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
Write \left(\frac{\pi}{4}e^{-\mathtt{C}r_{\star}-\mathtt{C}}\right) as some positive constant \mathtt{c}. The left-hand side of (3.17) is thus bounded below by:
\left(\mathtt{c}\alpha-(\mathtt{C}+1)e^{\mathtt{C}r_{\star}}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
For \alpha large enough, we have \mathtt{c}\alpha-(\mathtt{C}+1)e^{\mathtt{C}r_{\star}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\mathtt{c}\alpha, which concludes the proof of Claim 3.4.
∎
This last step only works for a fixed radius of the shell. For “higher” shells, we use a rough lower bound.
Step 3. A lower bound for higher shells.
Claim 3.5.
If x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\setminus\{0\}, t\in[0,1], and \mathrm{Q}_{x} is supported on \{u,|u|\leq\varepsilon\} for some \varepsilon>0, we have:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(2\pi\alpha\left|(x+tu)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\right|^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|x+tu|^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\geq-e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+2\pi\alpha|x|\varepsilon}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right).
(3.18)
Proof.
We simply discard the positive contribution, and write: e^{-\pi\alpha|x+tu|^{2}}\leq e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+2\pi\alpha|x|\varepsilon}.
∎
Since we assume here that \|\mathbf{p}\| is smaller than \frac{1}{\alpha}, we can take \varepsilon=\frac{2}{\alpha} in (3.18) and get:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(2\pi\alpha\left|(x+tu)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\right|^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|x+tu|^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\geq-e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi|x|}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right).
(3.19)
Combining (3.9), (3.10), (3.12), (3.16), (3.17) and (3.19), and integrating over t, we find that, for some small constant \mathtt{c}>0, provided \alpha is large enough, the quantity \mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) is bounded below by:
2\pi\alpha\left(\mathtt{c}\alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p})-\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>r_{\star}}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi|x|}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right)\right).
(3.20)
We want to argue that, for \alpha large enough, the second sum in (3.20) is dominated by the first one because of the quickly decreasing Gaussian weight. However, we also need to compare the values of \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u) for x in the first shell, which contribute to \mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}) (see (3.1)), and its values in “higher” shells.
Step 4. Comparing relative displacements far and close to the origin.
Claim 3.6.
For x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}, with |x|>r_{\star}, we have:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\leq\left(\frac{|x|}{r_{\star}}\right)^{2}\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.21)
Proof.
This is easy to see with the probabilistic formulation, for which (see (2.9)):
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)=\mathbb{E}\left[|\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}|^{2}\right],
where \mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}} is the \mathsf{A}_{2}-stationary random perturbation defined in (2.7). Pick a lattice point x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}, there exists n\leq\frac{|x|}{r_{\star}} and a path 0=x_{1},\dots,x_{n}=x within \mathsf{A}_{2} such that x_{i+1}-x_{i} belongs to the first shell S^{\star} for all i=0,\dots,n-1. We have, using Cauchy-Schwarz, the stationarity of \mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}, and a rough upper bound:
\mathbb{E}\left[|\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}|^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x_{i+1}}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x_{i}}\right|^{2}\right]\leq n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x_{i+1}}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x_{i}}\right|^{2}\right]\\
=n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x_{i+1}-x_{i}}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}\right|^{2}\right]\leq n^{2}\sum_{x\in S^{\star}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}\right|^{2}\right].
∎
Step 5. Proof of (3.5).
Inserting (3.21) into (3.20), we find:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq 2\pi\alpha\left(\mathtt{c}\alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}-\frac{1}{r_{\star}^{2}}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>r_{\star}}|x|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi|x|}\right)\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
As \alpha\to\infty, we have \sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>r_{\star}}|x|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi|x|}=o(e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}) which concludes the proof of (3.5) with an extra factor \alpha^{2}, which we discard for clarity (here \alpha is bounded below by 1).
This yields local optimality of \mathsf{A}_{2} with respect to Gaussian potentials that are “very peaked”, and are thus essentially nearest-neighbor interactions. The main ingredient is our “periodic 2-design inequality”, which basically leverages the lattice symmetry to ensure that some Hessian is positive.
We conclude the proof of Lemma 3.2 by proving (3.6). We now only assume that \|\mathbf{p}\| satisfies (1.3).
Step 6. A general lower bound.
We proceed as above: for each x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\setminus\{0\}, use the Taylor expansion (3.10) and insert the expression (3.12) for the second derivative. Then, discard the positive contribution and simply use the rough lower bound (3.18) with \varepsilon=2\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{10}. We get:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq-\mathtt{C}\alpha\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},x\neq 0}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+\frac{1}{5}\pi\alpha|x|r_{\star}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right).
(3.22)
Inserting (3.21), we can actually write this lower bound in terms of \mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}):
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq-\mathtt{C}\alpha\left(\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},x\neq 0}|x|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+\frac{1}{5}\pi\alpha|x|r_{\star}}\right)\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
For \alpha large enough, the sum is dominated by the contribution of the first shell, which yields
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq-\mathtt{C}\alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}+\frac{1}{5}\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}),
and since \alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}+\frac{1}{5}\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}=o(e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}) as \alpha\to\infty, we get (3.6).
In conclusion, we can choose \alpha_{\dagger}\geq 1 large enough such that (3.5) and (3.6) hold for \alpha\geq\alpha_{\dagger}.
3.2 Second case: \alpha small.
We now assume that \alpha\in(0,\alpha_{\dagger}), where \alpha_{\dagger} is the threshold fixed above. We start with the proof of (3.7).
Step 0. Decomposition into low and high layers.
Let R\geq 0 to be chosen later. We return to (3.9) and split the lattice sum into “low” and “high” layers, namely we write \mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})=\mathrm{Low}+\mathrm{High}:
\mathrm{Low}:=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|\leq R}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+u)-\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u),\quad\mathrm{High}:=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+u)-\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u).
We start with the \mathrm{Low} term (we can include x=0 in the sum, as its contribution is zero since \mathrm{Q}_{0}=\delta_{0}).
Step 1: Taylor expansion to third order.
For all x,u we can write:
\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+u)=\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)+\nabla\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u+\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)+\mathcal{O}(|u|^{3})\|\nabla^{3}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}\|_{\infty}.
By scaling, we have \|\nabla^{3}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}\|_{\infty}=\mathtt{C}\alpha^{\frac{3}{2}}. Integrating this expansion against \mathrm{Q}_{x} yields, for some \mathtt{C}>0:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+u)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\geq\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)-\mathtt{C}\|\mathbf{p}\|\alpha^{\frac{3}{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)
where we used the fact that \mathrm{Q}_{x} is centered, and supported on a disk of radius 2\|\mathbf{p}\|. We may thus write:
\mathrm{Low}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|\leq R}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)+\mathrm{ErrorLow}_{1},
(3.23)
with an error term satisfying:
\mathrm{ErrorLow}_{1}\geq-\mathtt{C}\|\mathbf{p}\|\alpha^{\frac{3}{2}}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|\leq R}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u).
(3.24)
Step 2: Re-introducing the missing layers.
Using (3.11), we know that for all x,u we have:
\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)=2\pi\alpha\left(2\pi\alpha\left|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\right|^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}}\leq 4\pi^{2}\alpha^{2}|x|^{2}|u|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}}.
(3.25)
We now simply re-introduce the missing layers in the sum over x in (3.23) and write:
\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|\leq R}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)-\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\\
\geq\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)-4\pi^{2}\alpha^{2}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}|x|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right).
(3.26)
Combining this with (3.23), (3.24), we write:
\mathrm{Low}=\mathrm{MainLow}+\mathrm{ErrorLow}_{2},
(3.27)
where \mathrm{MainLow} is the full lattice sum
\mathrm{MainLow}:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u),
(3.28)
and the error term is now such that:
\mathrm{ErrorLow}_{2}\geq-\mathtt{C}\|\mathbf{p}\|\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|\leq R}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)-\mathtt{C}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}|x|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right).
(3.29)
Remark 3.7.
In (3.29) we discarded some powers of \alpha (\alpha^{\frac{3}{2}} in front of the first sum and \alpha^{2} in front of the second one), and blended them into the multiplicative constant, which is valid because \alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger}. Those prefactors would only have a minor effect, as ultimately the main barrier to overcome is exponential in \frac{1}{\alpha}, so we prefer to not keep track of them.
In the next step, we focus on \mathrm{MainLow} and move to Fourier side using Poisson summation’s formula.
Step 3: Introducing the autocorrelation and the spectral measure(s).
For all x,u, write u=(u_{1},u_{2}) and \nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u) as:
\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)(u,u)=\sum_{a,b\in\{1,2\}}\partial^{2}_{ab}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)u_{a}u_{b},
(3.30)
and observe that, with the notation introduced in (2.10), (2.12), we have:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}u_{a}u_{b}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)=\mathrm{C}^{ab}=2\left[\mathrm{R}^{ab}_{0}-\mathrm{R}^{ab}_{x}\right],
(3.31)
where \mathrm{R} is the “autocorrelation” of \mathbf{p}. Combining (3.30), (3.31) and (3.28), we may thus write:
\mathrm{MainLow}=\sum_{a,b\in\{1,2\}}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}\partial^{2}_{ab}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)\left[\mathrm{R}^{ab}_{0}-\mathrm{R}^{ab}_{x}\right].
(3.32)
Since \mathsf{G}_{\alpha} is a Schwartz function, so are its derivatives. Moreover the autocorrelation is bounded, so we may apply Poisson’s summation formula, which gives, for each a,b\in\{1,2\}:
\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}\partial^{2}_{ab}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)\left[\mathrm{R}^{ab}_{0}-\mathrm{R}^{ab}_{x}\right]=\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}\widehat{\partial^{2}_{ab}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k)\times\mathrm{R}^{ab}_{0}-\widehat{\partial^{2}_{ab}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}\star\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}(k)
(3.33)
using the spectral measures \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab} introduced in Section 2.6. An elementary computation shows that:
\widehat{\partial^{2}_{ab}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k)=-4\pi^{2}\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k)k_{a}k_{b}
(3.34)
for all k and a,b\in\{1,2\}. Since \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab} is a measure on \Omega, we can write the convolution \widehat{\partial^{2}_{ab}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}\star\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab} as:
\widehat{\partial^{2}_{ab}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}\star\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}(k)=-4\pi^{2}\int_{\Omega}\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k+\omega)(k+\omega)_{a}(k+\omega)_{b}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}(\omega),
(3.35)
and we obtain, after summing over a,b\in\{1,2\} and over k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}:
\mathrm{MainLow}=4\pi^{2}\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}\sum_{a,b\in\{1,2\}}\left(\int_{\Omega}\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k+\omega)(k+\omega)_{a}(k+\omega)_{b}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}(\omega)-\mathrm{R}^{ab}_{0}\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k)k_{a}k_{b}\right).
(3.36)
We now combine the four coefficients \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab} of the matrix-valued spectral measure \widehat{\mathsf{R}}, introduce the trace measure \tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}} as in (2.14), and use the identity (2.15) to write
\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}\sum_{a,b\in\{1,2\}}\int_{\Omega}\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k+\omega)(k+\omega)_{a}(k+\omega)_{b}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}(\omega)\\
=\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}\int_{\Omega}\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k+\omega)\left(\lambda_{1}(\omega)\left((k+\omega)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v_{1}(\omega)\right)^{2}+\lambda_{2}(\omega)\left((k+\omega)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v_{2}(\omega)\right)^{2}\right)\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega),
where \lambda_{1},\lambda_{2} are the \omega-dependent eigenvalues of the “trace derivative” \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}(\omega), and v_{1},v_{2} its eigenvectors, forming an orthonormal basis.
On the other hand, using the fact that \mathrm{R}_{0}=\int_{\Omega}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}} by (2.13), and applying (2.15) again, we can write:
\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}\sum_{a,b\in\{1,2\}}\mathrm{R}^{ab}_{0}\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k)k_{a}k_{b}=\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}\sum_{a,b\in\{1,2\}}\int_{\Omega}\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k)k_{a}k_{b}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}(\omega)\\
=\int_{\Omega}\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k)\left(\lambda_{1}(\omega)\left(k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v_{1}(\omega)\right)^{2}+\lambda_{2}(\omega)\left(k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v_{2}(\omega)\right)^{2}\right)\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega).
Finally, recall that \widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}(k)=\alpha^{-1}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|k|^{2}} (see (2.1)) and introduce, as in (2.27), the function:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}:\omega\mapsto\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}|(k+\omega)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|k+\omega|^{2}}.
We obtain the following expression, where \lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},v_{1},v_{2} are functions of \omega:
\mathrm{MainLow}=4\pi^{2}\alpha^{-1}\left(\int_{\Omega}\left(\lambda_{1}\left(\Psi_{\alpha,v_{1}}(\omega)-\Psi_{\alpha,v_{1}}(0)\right)+\lambda_{2}\left(\Psi_{\alpha,v_{2}}(\omega)-\Psi_{\alpha,v_{2}}(0)\right)\right)\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\right).
(3.37)
Step 4: Coercivity of \mathrm{MainLow}.
By Proposition 2.12, we know that there exists \mathtt{c}>0 such that, for all \alpha\in(0,\alpha_{\dagger}), for all choices of v such that |v|=1, and all \omega\in\Omega:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}(\omega)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}|\omega|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(3.38)
We may thus write (recall that \lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}=1 almost everywhere, see Section 2.6):
\int_{\Omega}\left(\lambda_{1}\left(\Psi_{\alpha,v_{1}}(\omega)-\Psi_{\alpha,v_{1}}(0)\right)+\lambda_{2}\left(\Psi_{\alpha,v_{2}}(\omega)-\Psi_{\alpha,v_{2}}(0)\right)\right)\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{tr}\left(\int_{\Omega}|w|^{2}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\right).
Inserting this into (3.37), and using our notation \mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}) (see (3.2)), we obtain the following lower bound:
\mathrm{MainLow}\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}),
(3.39)
where we discarded the \alpha^{-1} factor for simplicity (here \alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger}). For all x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}, using Lemma 2.6 we get:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\leq\mathtt{C}|x|^{2}\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.40)
Inserting (3.40) into the expression (3.29) of \mathrm{ErrorLow}_{2}, this yields:
\mathrm{ErrorLow}_{2}\geq-\mathtt{C}\left(\|\mathbf{p}\|\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|\leq R}|x|^{2}+\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}|x|^{4}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}}\right)\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.41)
In conclusion, we have obtained \mathrm{Low}=\mathrm{MainLow}+\mathrm{ErrorLow}_{2}, with \mathrm{MainLow} as in (3.37), bounded below in terms of \mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}), while \mathrm{ErrorLow}_{2} is also bounded in terms of \mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}), see (3.39) and (3.41).
Next, we turn to the “high” layers, for which we use a simple, rough lower bound.
Step 5. A lower bound on the high layers.
Intuitively, if R is large enough compared to \alpha, the high layers (|x|>R) should not play an important role due to the decaying Gaussian weight. We use a rough lower bound on their contributions:
Claim 3.8.
We have
\mathrm{High}\geq-\mathtt{C}\alpha\left(\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}|x|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}\right)\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.42)
Proof.
We return to the Taylor expansion used in (3.10), and to the expression (3.12) for \nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}, we discard the positive contribution in \nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+tu)\left(u,u\right) and write, for all t\in[0,1] (cf. the proof of (3.22)):
\nabla^{2}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+tu)(u,u)\geq-2\pi\alpha|u|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi\alpha|x|\|\mathbf{p}\|}.
We thus have, using (3.40) in the second inequality:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x+u)-\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\geq-\mathtt{C}\alpha\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi\alpha|x|\|\mathbf{p}\|}\\
\geq-\mathtt{C}\alpha|x|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi\alpha|x|\|\mathbf{p}\|}\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.43)
We now use again the fact that e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi\alpha|x|\|\mathbf{p}\|}\leq e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}. Summing over |x|>R yields (3.42).
∎
Step 6. Combining low and high layers
In summary, we have obtained:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})=\mathrm{Low}+\mathrm{High},\quad\mathrm{Low}\geq\mathrm{MainLow}+\mathrm{ErrorLow}_{2},
(3.44)
where \mathrm{MainLow}, \mathrm{ErrorLow}_{2} and \mathrm{High} are all bounded in terms of \mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}), see (3.39), (3.41) and (3.42). In those last two bounds, there is a lattice sum over the “high layers” |x|>R:
\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}|x|^{4}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}}\text{ in \eqref{ErrorLow2B} },\quad\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}\alpha|x|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}\text{ in \eqref{eq:LBHighLayers} }.
For simplicity, we bound combine them into a common bound:
\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}|x|^{4}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}}+\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}\alpha|x|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}\leq\mathtt{C}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}|x|^{4}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}.
(recall that \alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger}, and that |x|^{2}\leq\mathtt{C}|x|^{4} because even if R=0, we have |x|\geq r_{\star}). We then get:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\\
\mathtt{c}\left(e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}-\mathtt{C}_{1}\|\mathbf{p}\|\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|\leq R}|x|^{2}-\mathtt{C}_{1}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}|x|^{4}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}\right)\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}),
(3.45)
for some constant \mathtt{C}_{1} independent on \alpha\in(0,\alpha_{\dagger}). The positive term in the parenthesis comes from \mathrm{MainLow}, see (3.39), and the two negative ones from the lower bounds on \mathrm{ErrorLow}_{2} and \mathrm{High}.
Step 7. Choosing R.
We now take R of the form \frac{M}{\alpha}, with M “large”. By comparing the lattice sum to a Gaussian integral, we see that there exists \mathtt{C}_{0}>0 such that, for all \alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger} and all R\geq\frac{\mathtt{C}_{0}}{\alpha}:
\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>R}|x|^{4}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}\leq\mathtt{C}R^{4}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}R^{2}}.
We thus see that, uniformly for M\geq\mathtt{C}_{0} and for \alpha\in(0,\alpha_{\dagger}):
\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>\frac{M}{\alpha}}|x|^{4}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}\leq\mathtt{C}\alpha^{-4}M^{4}e^{-\frac{\pi M^{2}}{2\alpha}}\leq\mathtt{C}^{\prime}M^{4}e^{-\frac{\pi M^{2}}{4\alpha}}.
Choosing M large enough, we can then ensure, for all \alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger}:
\mathtt{C}_{1}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>\frac{M}{\alpha}}|x|^{4}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}\leq\mathtt{C}_{1}\mathtt{C}^{\prime}M^{4}e^{-\frac{\pi M^{2}}{4\alpha}}\leq\frac{1}{4}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(3.46)
Moreover, we our choice R=\frac{M}{\alpha}, we have the upper bound:
\|\mathbf{p}\|\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|\leq\frac{M}{\alpha}}|x|^{2}\leq\mathtt{C}{{}^{\prime\prime}}\|\mathbf{p}\|M^{4}\alpha^{-4}.
(3.47)
Our condition \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}} with \mathtt{c} small enough ensures that, for \alpha\in(0,\alpha_{\dagger}):
\mathtt{C}_{1}\|\mathbf{p}\|\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|\leq R}|x|^{2}\leq\mathtt{c}\mathtt{C}_{1}\mathtt{C}{{}^{\prime\prime}}M^{4}\alpha^{-4}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{4}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(3.48)
Inserting the controls (3.46) and (3.48) into (3.45), we obtain (3.7)
We conclude the proof of Lemma 3.3 by proving (3.8). We now only assume that \|\mathbf{p}\| satisfies (1.3).
Step 8. Proof of (3.8)
We choose R=0, so there are only “high” layers, and we use (3.42), which gives:
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq-\mathtt{C}\alpha\left(\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}|x|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}|x|^{2}}\right)\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}).
For \alpha\in(0,\alpha_{\dagger}), the sum is bounded by \mathtt{C}\alpha^{-2} (this can be seen e.g. by applying Poisson’s summation formula, or by comparing to a Gaussian integral), which yields (3.8).
3.3 Local optimality for c.m.s.d. functions: proof of Theorem 2
Let f be a c.m.s.d function and let \mathrm{W}_{f} be the associated measure on [0,+\infty), such that
f=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\Phi_{\alpha}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha).
In this section, we find conditions on \mathrm{W}_{f} ensuring the existence of \varepsilon>0 such that for all periodic perturbations \mathbf{p}:
\text{If }\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon\text{ then }\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\geq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}).
Moreover, we observe that the choice of \varepsilon can be done uniformly on certain families of functions f, as stated in Theorem 2. The starting point is to write:
\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2})=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\left(\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha),
which should be quickly justified: if f is a c.m.s.d function such that x\mapsto f(|x|) is integrable at infinity (otherwise \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) and \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}) are infinite, see Remark 1.1) then the \liminf’s defining \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}),\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}) in (1.1) are limits, and we simply write:
\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})=\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r},x\neq y}\int_{0}^{+\infty}\Phi_{\alpha}(|x-y|)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\\
=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\left(\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r},x\neq y}\Phi_{\alpha}(|x-y|)\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha).
Step 1. Selecting \varepsilon for the large \alpha’s
Let \alpha_{\dagger} be the threshold given by Lemma 3.2. We first focus on the contributions coming from \alpha\geq\alpha_{\dagger}.
Claim 3.9 (Large \alpha’s).
Let \alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{\dagger} to be chosen later, and assume that \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha_{1}}. We have:
\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{+\infty}\left(\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\\
\geq\left(\mathtt{c}\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)-\mathtt{C}\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\right)\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.49)
Proof.
We split the integral into two parts:
•
For \alpha between \alpha_{\dagger} and \alpha_{1}, since we assume that \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha_{1}}\leq\frac{1}{\alpha} we can use our quantitative local minimality statement (3.5) and integrate it over \alpha, which yields:
\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{\alpha_{1}}\left(\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\geq\mathtt{c}\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{\alpha_{1}}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
•
If \alpha\geq\alpha_{1}, we use instead the rough lower bound (3.6), which gives:
\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}\left(\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\geq-\mathtt{C}\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
We also write, for simplicity:
\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{\alpha_{1}}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)=\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)-\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\\
\geq\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)-\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha).
We obtain (3.49).
∎
Next, we focus on the contributions to \mathrm{E}_{f} coming from \alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger}.
Step 2. Selecting \varepsilon for the small \alpha’s
Claim 3.10.
Let 0<\alpha_{0}\leq\alpha_{\dagger} to be chosen later, and assume that \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\mathtt{c}_{1}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha_{0}}r_{\star}^{2}} with \mathtt{c}_{1} the constant appearing in Lemma 3.3. We have:
\int_{0}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}\left(\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\geq\left(\mathtt{c}_{1}\int_{0}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)-\mathtt{C}\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\right)\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.50)
Proof.
We split again the integral into two parts:
•
If \alpha is between \alpha_{0} and \alpha_{\dagger}, since we assume that \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\mathtt{c}_{1}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha_{0}}r_{\star}^{2}}\leq\mathtt{c}_{1}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}, we can use our quantitative local minimality bound (3.7), which yields:
\int_{\alpha_{0}}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}\left(\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\geq\mathtt{c}_{1}\int_{\alpha_{0}}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
•
If \alpha is smaller than \alpha_{0}, we use instead the rough lower bound (3.8), which gives:
\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}\left(\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\geq-\mathtt{C}\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}\alpha^{-1}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
Again, for simplicity, we write:
\int_{\alpha_{0}}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)=\int_{0}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)-\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\\
\geq\int_{0}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)-\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\geq\int_{0}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)-\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}\alpha^{-1}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha),
and we obtain (3.50).
∎
Step 3. Conclusion
In summary, for all \alpha_{0}\leq\alpha_{\dagger}\leq\alpha_{1}, assuming that
\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\min\left(\frac{1}{\alpha_{1}},\mathtt{c}_{1}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha_{0}}r_{\star}^{2}}\right),
(3.51)
we obtain the following lower bound on \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) (recall that \mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}) controls \mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}) by (2.17)):
\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\Bigg(\mathtt{c}\left(\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\right)\\
-\mathtt{C}\left(\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}\alpha^{-1}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\right)\Bigg)\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).
(3.52)
We make two observations:
1.
By definition, for all r>0, the integral \int_{0}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)=f(r) is finite, so in particular \alpha\mapsto e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}} is \mathrm{W}_{f}-integrable at infinity.
2.
The condition \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2})<+\infty is equivalent to r\mapsto rf(r) being integrable at infinity, see Remark 1.1. A direct computation shows that:
\int_{1}^{+\infty}rf(r)\mathtt{d}r=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\int_{1}^{+\infty}re^{-\pi\alpha r^{2}}\mathtt{d}r\ \mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\alpha^{-1}\int_{\sqrt{\alpha}}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi u^{2}}\mathtt{d}u\ \mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha),
(3.53)
and thus this finiteness condition implies that \alpha\mapsto\alpha^{-1} must be \mathrm{W}_{f}-integrable near 0.
As a consequence, by choosing \alpha_{1} large enough and \alpha_{0} small enough (depending on f), we can ensure that the parenthesis in (3.52) is positive. Taking \varepsilon as the right-hand side of (3.51), and imposing \|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon, we deduce that \mathsf{A}_{2} is locally optimal for \mathrm{E}_{f}. This proves the first statement in Theorem 2.
Moreover, we see that \alpha_{0},\alpha_{1} can be chosen uniformly over families \mathcal{F} of c.m.s.d functions f such that:
\lim_{\alpha_{0}\to 0,\alpha_{1}\to\infty}\frac{\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}\alpha^{-1}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)}{\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)}=0\text{ uniformly for $f\in\mathcal{F}$.}
Here \alpha_{\dagger}\geq 1 is the threshold from Lemma 3.2, for which we never searched an explicit value. For simplicity, we replace it by 1 in the integral bounds, which is valid because:
\int_{1}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{1}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\leq\mathtt{C}\left(\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{\alpha_{\dagger}}\alpha^{-1}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\right),
indeed, e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}, e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}} are comparable for \alpha\in[1,\alpha_{\dagger}]. This concludes the proof of Theorem 2.
Appendix A Reduction to periodic perturbations: proof of Lemma 2.1
Let f be a c.m.s.d function - in particular, f is smooth and decreasing. Without loss of generality, we can assume that x\mapsto f(|x|) (or equivalently r\mapsto rf(r)) is integrable at \infty, otherwise both \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) and \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}) are infinite and there is nothing to prove.
For N\geq 1, let \mathsf{L}_{N} be the sub-lattice of \mathsf{A}_{2} generated by the vectors 2N\sigma and 2N\tau, and let \Lambda_{N} be a fundamental domain (here a parallelogram) for \mathsf{L}_{N} given by \Lambda_{N}:=\left\{sN\sigma+tN\tau,\ (s,t)\in[-1,1]^{2}\right\}.
The sequence of shapes (\Lambda_{N})_{N\geq 1} converges to \mathbb{R}^{2} in the sense of Van Hove, see [FV17, Sec. 3.2.1]. It is folklore that the following limit exists (see e.g. [BL15, Sec. 2.4]):
\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r},x\neq y}f(|x-y|),
cf. (1.1), and coincides with the same limit taken along the sequence (\Lambda_{N})_{N\geq 1}, thus we have:
\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N},\ x\neq y}f(|x-y|).
(A.1)
In particular, we can take N large enough such that:
