\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N},x\neq y}f(|x-y|)\leq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})+\delta.
(A.2)
We restrict \mathbf{p} to the parallelogram \Lambda_{N}, and define \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}} as the \mathsf{L}_{N}-periodic extension of \mathbf{p} to \mathsf{A}_{2}. Of course, we have \|\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}}\|\leq\|\mathbf{p}\|. It remains to prove that \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}}) is not much larger than \mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}).
Consider the sub-sequence of shapes (\Lambda_{kN})_{k\geq 1}. For the same reason as above, we have:
\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{kN}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{kN},\ x\neq y}f(|x-y|).
(A.3)
Notice that \Lambda_{kN} is the disjoint union of k^{2} disjoint copies of \Lambda_{N}. Since \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}} is periodic by construction, and coincides with \mathbf{p} on \Lambda_{N}, we have:
|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{kN}|=k^{2}|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N}|.
Moreover, the energy within \Lambda_{kN} is given by k^{2} times the energy within \Lambda_{N}, plus the interactions between each copy of \Lambda_{N} and the rest of the configuration. Since f is decreasing and x\mapsto f(|x|) is integrable at infinity, we have, for x\in\Lambda_{N}
\sum_{y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\setminus\Lambda_{N}}|f(x-y)|=o_{\mathrm{dist}(x,\partial\Lambda_{N})\to\infty}(1),
and thus we can bound the interaction between each copy and the rest of the configuration by:
\sum_{x\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{N},y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\setminus\Lambda_{N}}\left|f(|x-y|)\right|=o\left(|\Lambda_{N}|\right),
using the fact that boundary contributions are negligible with respect to the volume. In particular, choosing N large enough, we have:
\frac{1}{|\Lambda_{N}|}\sum_{x\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{N},y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\setminus\Lambda_{N}}|f(x-y)|\leq\delta,
which in particular implies for all k\geq 1:
\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{kN},\ x\neq y}f(|x-y|)\leq k^{2}\times\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N},\ x\neq y}f(|x-y|)+k^{2}\delta.
Dividing by |(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{kN}|=k^{2}|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N}|, inserting (A.2), and sending k\to\infty (see (A.3)) yields the result.
Appendix B Proof of the “geometric” Lemma 2.10
Without loss of generality, we assume that S has sidelength r=1. For k,v fixed, we want to prove:
\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}\left(\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)\right)|v|^{2},\quad\text{ with }w_{s}(k):=2\left(1-\cos\left(2\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s\right)\right).
This can be rewritten in “linear algebraic” terms as:
\mathrm{M}v\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v\geq\frac{1}{4}|v|^{2},\quad\text{ where }\mathrm{M}:=\frac{1}{\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u)}\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)ss^{T}.
(B.1)
The matrix \mathrm{M} is positive symmetric as a mixture of orthogonal projections. We can write it down explicitly using the fact that the vertices of S are given by:
s_{1}:=(1,0),\quad s_{2}:=\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right),\quad s_{3}=s_{2}-s_{1}=\left(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right),
together with their opposites, which yield the same contributions.
We obtain:
\mathrm{M}=\frac{1}{w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{3}}\begin{pmatrix}w_{1}+\tfrac{w_{2}+w_{3}}{4}&\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(w_{2}-w_{3})\\[2.84526pt]
\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(w_{2}-w_{3})&\tfrac{3}{4}(w_{2}+w_{3})\end{pmatrix}
where we write w_{1},w_{2},w_{3} instead of w_{s_{1}}(k),w_{s_{2}}(k),w_{s_{3}}(k). Clearly, \mathtt{tr}\mathrm{M}=1, and \det\mathrm{M} is given by
\det\mathrm{M}=\frac{3}{4}\frac{w_{1}w_{2}+w_{2}w_{3}+w_{1}w_{3}}{(w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{3})^{2}}.
(B.2)
An elementary computation shows that the smallest eigenvalue \lambda_{\min} of \mathrm{M} is then equal to
\lambda_{\min}=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4\det\mathrm{M}}}{2}.
Proving that \lambda_{\min}\geq\frac{1}{4} will imply (B.1). By our expression (B.2) for \det\mathrm{M}, this is equivalent to having:
\frac{w_{1}w_{2}+w_{2}w_{3}+w_{1}w_{3}}{(w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{3})^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{4}.
(B.3)
Such an inequality is of course false if w_{1},w_{2},w_{3} are arbitrary positive numbers, because one of them could be much larger than the other two, making the ratio very small. We now claim that since s_{3}=s_{2}-s_{1}, there cannot be one term among w_{1},w_{2},w_{3} which is much larger than the other two.
Claim B.1.
We have:
w_{1}w_{2}+w_{2}w_{3}+w_{1}w_{3}\geq\frac{1}{4}(w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{3})^{2}.
(B.4)
Proof.
For j\in\{1,2,3\} let \theta_{j}:=2\pi s_{j}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k and let c_{j}:=\cos\theta_{j}. We have by definition:
w_{j}=2\left(1-c_{j}\right)=4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{j}}{2}\right).
The inequality (B.4) can then be re-written, after some algebra, as:
4\left(c_{1}c_{2}+c_{2}c_{3}+c_{3}c_{1}\right)-\left(c_{1}+c_{2}+c_{3}\right)^{2}-2\left(c_{1}+c_{2}+c_{3}\right)+3\geq 0.
(B.5)
Introduce the auxiliary variable t:=\sin\left(\theta_{1}\right)\sin\left(\theta_{2}\right). Since s_{3}=s_{2}-s_{1} as vectors, we have:
c_{3}=\cos\left(\theta_{3}\right)=\cos\left(2\pi s_{3}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k\right)=\cos\left(2\pi(s_{2}-s_{1})\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k\right)=\cos(\theta_{2}-\theta_{1})=c_{1}c_{2}+\sin(\theta_{1})\sin(\theta_{2})=c_{1}c_{2}+t.
Injecting this, and noticing that t^{2}=(1-c_{1}^{2})(1-c_{2}^{2}), we can re-write the left-hand side of (B.5) as:
4\left(c_{1}c_{2}+c_{2}c_{3}+c_{3}c_{1}\right)-\left(c_{1}+c_{2}+c_{3}\right)^{2}-2\left(c_{1}+c_{2}+c_{3}\right)+3\\
=4\left(1-c_{1}\right)\left(1-c_{2}\right)-\left(t+(1-c_{1})(1-c_{2})\right)^{2}.
(B.6)
Finally, some elementary trigonometry yields:
\left(1-c_{1}\right)\left(1-c_{2}\right)=4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}\right)\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{2}}{2}\right),\quad t+(1-c_{1})(1-c_{2})=4\sin\left(\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\theta_{2}}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}}{2}\right).
The inequality (B.5) expresses that the right-hand side of (B.6) is non-negative, and is thus equivalent to:
16\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}\right)\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{2}}{2}\right)-16\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}\right)\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{2}}{2}\right)\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}}{2}\right)\geq 0,
which is true, and concludes the proof of the claim.
∎
Now, the inequality (B.4) being satisfied, we get (B.1), which yields the result.
Appendix C Proof of Proposition 2.12
Recall that v is a fixed unit vector and that \Psi_{\alpha,v} is defined on the fundamental domain \mathcal{H} of \mathsf{A}_{2} by:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}:u\mapsto\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}|(x+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|x+u|^{2}}.
(C.1)
We want to show that \Psi_{\alpha} is minimal at 0, with a lower bound of the form \Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}|u|^{2}.
\mathcal{H}\tfrac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}0
Figure 2: A close-up of the fundamental hexagon \mathcal{H}, surrounded by the first “shell” of the lattice.
We will use the following numerical constants:
r_{\star}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}}\approx 1.0746,\quad\bar{\alpha}:=0.552.
We distinguish between two ranges for \alpha: “large” (between \bar{\alpha} and \alpha_{\dagger}) and “small” (between 0 and \bar{\alpha}).
C.1 First case: \alpha large.
Lemma C.1.
Let \alpha_{\dagger} be fixed. There exists \mathtt{c}>0 such that for all \alpha\in(\bar{\alpha},\alpha_{\dagger}), for all unit vector v, and all u in \mathcal{H}, we have:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}|u|^{2}.
(C.2)
Proof.
Assume that \alpha\in(\bar{\alpha},\alpha_{\dagger}) and fix a unit vector v.
Step 1. Moving to Fourier side.
Taking the Fourier transform of x\mapsto|(x+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|x+u|^{2}} in \mathbb{R}^{2}, for u\in\mathbb{R}^{2} fixed and |v|=1 yields:
k\mapsto\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2\pi}\left(1-2\pi\alpha|k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|k|^{2}}e^{2i\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k},
and thus, applying Poisson’s summation formula, for all u\in\mathcal{H} we have the identity:
\Psi_{\alpha}(u)=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2\pi}\left(1+\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2},k\neq 0}\left(1-2\pi\alpha|k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|k|^{2}}\cos(2\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k)\right),
(C.3)
and thus in particular, we can write the difference \Psi_{\alpha}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha}(0) as:
\Psi_{\alpha}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha}(0)=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2\pi}\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2},k\neq 0}\left(2\pi\alpha|k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}-1\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|k|^{2}}\left(1-\cos(2\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k)\right).
(C.4)
Step 2. Using the periodic 2-design property.
Fix a shell S of radius r>0 within \widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} and write:
\sum_{s\in S}\left(2\pi\alpha|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}-1\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|s|^{2}}\left(1-\cos(2\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s)\right)=\left(\pi\alpha\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u)|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u)\right)e^{-\pi\alpha r^{2}},
(C.5)
with non-negative weights w_{s}(u)=2\left(1-\cos(2\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s)\right) as in (2.22). Applying Lemma 2.10 we get:
\pi\alpha\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u)|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u)\geq\left(\frac{1}{4}\pi\alpha r^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u)=\frac{1}{4}\pi r^{2}\left(\alpha-\frac{2}{\pi r^{2}}\right)\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u).
(C.6)
Since r\geq r_{\star}, since we assume \alpha\geq\bar{\alpha}, and since the following numerical inequality is true:
\bar{\alpha}>\frac{2}{\pi r_{\star}^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\quad(0.552>0.55132..)
(C.7)
the right-hand side of (C.6) is non-negative, thus so is (C.5).
Step 3. Quadratic lower bound.
All the shells have a positive contribution, we focus on the first one.
Claim C.2.
For all u\in\mathcal{H}, we have, S^{\star} being the first shell of the lattice \widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}:
\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}w_{s}(u)\geq 48r_{\star}^{2}|u|^{2}.
(C.8)
Proof.
By the choice of the fundamental cell \mathcal{H}, we have |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s|\leq\frac{1}{2} for all s\in S^{\star} and u\in\mathcal{H}. Using the lower bound 1-\cos x\geq\frac{2}{\pi^{2}}x^{2} valid for |x|\leq\pi, we get:
w_{s}(u)=2\left(1-\cos(2\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s)\right)\geq 16|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s|^{2}.
Summing over the six vertices of S^{\star} and using the 2-design property (2.18), we get (C.8).
∎
Combining (C.5), (C.6) and (C.8) we obtain:
\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}\left(2\pi\alpha|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}-1\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|s|^{2}}\left(1-\cos(2\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s)\right)\geq 12\pi r_{\star}^{4}\left(\alpha-\frac{2}{\pi r_{\star}^{2}}\right)|u|^{2}.
(C.9)
Returning to (C.4) and keeping only the first shell as a lower bound, we thus get:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq 6\alpha^{2}r_{\star}^{4}\left(\alpha-\frac{2}{\pi r_{\star}^{2}}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}|u|^{2}.
For \alpha\geq\bar{\alpha}>\frac{2}{\pi r_{\star}^{2}}, we can write, for some small universal constant \mathtt{c}
6r_{\star}^{4}\left(\alpha-\frac{2}{\pi r_{\star}^{2}}\right)\geq\mathtt{c}\alpha.
We have thus obtained
\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}\alpha^{3}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}|u|^{2}.
It is more convenient for us to re-write this as in (C.2). This is valid because, for \alpha between \bar{\alpha} and \alpha_{\dagger}:
\alpha^{3}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
∎
C.2 Second case: \alpha small.
Returning to the original expression (C.1) for \Psi_{\alpha,v}, we write for u\in\mathcal{H}:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)=|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}+\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\setminus\{0\}}|(x+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|x+u|^{2}},\quad\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\setminus\{0\}}|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|x|^{2}}.
(C.10)
Until the end of the proof, we assume that \alpha is “small” in the sense:
\alpha\leq\bar{\alpha}:=0.552
(C.11)
and our goal is to prove, for some constant \mathtt{c}>0 independent of \alpha,u:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}|u|^{2}.
(C.12)
The proof uses only elementary tools but is a bit intricate. We treat the first shell (and the origin) and the higher shells separately, and then distinguish several regimes in each case.
C.3 The first shell and the origin
Let S^{\star} be the first shell of \mathsf{A}_{2}. We denote by \Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star} the contribution coming from S^{\star}\cup\{0\}:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}:u\mapsto|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}+\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}|(s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}.
Using the 2-design property (2.18), for every shell S of radius r we have
\sum_{s\in S}|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s|^{2}}=3r^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r^{2}},
so we are interested in finding a lower bound of the form:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)=|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}+\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}|(s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}-3r_{\star}^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(C.13)
We will consider three cases:
1.
If |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “large”, a direct computation suffices.
2.
If |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “small” and |u| is “small”, we use a Taylor expansion.
3.
If |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “small” and |u| is “large”, direct or perturbative computations fail. We identify a “good vertex” within the first shell and show that its contribution is always big enough for (C.12) to hold. This relies on a tedious identification of the “worst case scenario” among all possible parameters.
Some of the arguments below rely on purely numerical inequalities between certain explicit quantities. A Python notebook that checks those inequalities is available here.
C.4 First situation: |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is large.
This first part deals only with the contribution of the origin. We make a simple observation:
Claim C.3 (If |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “large”.).
There exists a constant \mathtt{c}>0 such that the following holds. Assume that u,\alpha,v are such that:
|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\geq\sqrt{3.01}r_{\star}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\left(|u|^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)},
(C.14)
then we have:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(C.15)
Proof.
Discarding the contribution from the first shell and keeping only the one from 0 in (C.13), we get:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}-3r_{\star}^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}=\left(|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}\left(r_{\star}^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)}-3r_{\star}^{2}\right)e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
Our assumption (C.14) ensures that
|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}\left(r_{\star}^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)}\geq 3.01r_{\star}^{2},
so in particular, for some small constant \mathtt{c}>0 we can guarantee that, as stated in (C.15):
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}r_{\star}^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
∎
In the sequel, when considering \Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}, we may thus assume that |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is not “large” as in (C.14).
C.5 Second situation: |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is small and |u| is small.
We now turn to the case where |u| is small compared to \alpha, in the sense that \frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|\leq\mu_{\star}, for a certain threshold \mu_{\star}.
Lemma C.4.
There exists \mathtt{c}>0 such that the following holds.
Assume that u,v,\alpha are such that:
\alpha\leq\bar{\alpha},\quad|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\leq\sqrt{3.01}r_{\star}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\left(|u|^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)},\quad\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|\leq\mu_{\star}=2.73.
(C.16)
Then we have:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(C.17)
Proof.
We will prove that
\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}|(s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}-3r_{\star}^{2}\geq 0.01|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}},
(C.18)
which clearly implies (C.17). Expand the squares in the summands of (C.18) and write, for s\in S^{\star}:
((s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}=\left((s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}+2(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)+(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}\right)e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(C.19)
We focus first on the s-dependent part of the sum, namely:
\mathsf{Sum}:=\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}\left((s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}+2(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)+(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}\right)e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u}.
(C.20)
Step 1. A Taylor expansion to third order.
Using the following elementary lower bound:
e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u}\geq\sum_{k=0}^{3}\frac{1}{k!}\left(-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\right)^{k},
we see that \mathsf{Sum}\geq\mathsf{F}_{\mathrm{3}}, where \mathsf{F}_{\mathrm{3}} is the “third order Taylor Expansion” of \mathsf{Sum}, namely
\mathsf{F}_{\mathrm{3}}:=\sum_{k=0}^{3}\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}\left((s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}+2(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)+|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\right)\left(-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\right)^{k}.
(C.21)
By symmetry of S^{\star} with respect to s\mapsto-s, the sums with an odd total power in s vanish. Moreover, we can use the following identities due to the symmetries of a regular hexagon:
•
By the 2-design property (2.18), we have:
\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}=3r_{\star}^{2},\quad\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}=3r_{\star}^{2}|u|^{2},\quad\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)=3r_{\star}^{2}(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)
•
By the 4-design property stated in Remark 2.8, we have
\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}=\frac{3}{4}r_{\star}^{4}|u|^{2}+\frac{3}{2}r_{\star}^{4}(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2},\quad,\quad\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{3}=\frac{9}{4}r_{\star}^{4}(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)|u|^{2},\quad\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{4}=\frac{9}{4}r_{\star}^{4}|u|^{4}.
In the sequel, we use
\mathrm{K}:=\frac{\pi}{\alpha}
Expanding the right-hand side of (C.21), and using the identities above, we get:
\mathsf{F}_{\mathrm{3}}=3r_{\star}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{K}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}|u|^{2}+(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}\left(6+3\mathrm{K}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}\left(1-2\mathrm{K}|u|^{2}\right)+6\mathrm{K}r_{\star}^{2}\left(\mathrm{K}|u|^{2}-2\right)\right).
(C.22)
The following term might give a negative contribution:
\Gamma:=6+3\mathrm{K}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}\left(1-2\mathrm{K}|u|^{2}\right)+6\mathrm{K}r_{\star}^{2}\left(\mathrm{K}|u|^{2}-2\right).
Step 2. Preliminaries
Using the first and third constraints in (C.16) and our notation, we have:
\mathrm{K}\geq\mathrm{K}_{0}:=\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}\approx 5.691,\quad|u|\leq\frac{\mu_{\star}}{\mathrm{K}}.
Moreover, from the second condition in (C.16) we know that:
(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}\leq 3.01r_{\star}^{2}e^{\mathrm{K}\left(|u|^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)}
Using the variable y:=|u|^{2}, we thus have:
\mathsf{F}_{\mathrm{3}}\geq 3r_{\star}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{K}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}y+A(\mathrm{K},y)\min\left(0,\Gamma(\mathrm{K},y)\right),
where
y\leq y_{\max}(\mathrm{K}):=\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}^{2}},\quad A(\mathrm{K},y):=3.01r_{\star}^{2}e^{\mathrm{K}\left(y-r_{\star}^{2}\right)},\quad\Gamma(\mathrm{K},y):=\left(6+3\mathrm{K}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}\left(1-2\mathrm{K}y\right)+6\mathrm{K}r_{\star}^{2}\left(\mathrm{K}y-2\right)\right).
Observe that:
•
\partial_{y}\Gamma is always negative, because \mathrm{K}r_{\star}^{2}\geq\mathrm{K}_{0}r_{\star}^{2}>1, and \partial^{2}_{yy}\Gamma=0.
•
\Gamma(\mathrm{K},0)=3\left(2+\mathrm{K}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}-4\mathrm{K}r_{\star}^{2}\right) is positive because \mathrm{K}\geq\mathrm{K}_{0}\geq\frac{\left(2+\sqrt{2}\right)}{r_{\star}^{2}}, which is the largest root.
•
\partial_{y}A=\mathrm{K}A and \partial^{2}_{yy}A=\mathrm{K}^{2}A
Step 3. Concavity
Consider the function
\Phi(\mathrm{K},y):=3r_{\star}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{K}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}y+A(\mathrm{K},y)\min\left(0,\Gamma(\mathrm{K},y)\right)-3r_{\star}^{2}e^{\mathrm{K}y}-0.01ye^{\mathrm{K}y}.
We want to prove that \Phi\geq 0 for all admissible values of \mathrm{K},y. Clearly, we have \Phi(\mathrm{K},0)=0 for all \mathrm{K}. We claim that \Phi is concave with respect to the second variable. Indeed:
•
On \{\Gamma\geq 0\}, we have:
\partial^{2}_{yy}\Phi=-3r_{\star}^{2}\mathrm{K}^{2}e^{\mathrm{K}y}-0.01\left(2\mathrm{K}e^{\mathrm{K}y}+\mathrm{K}^{2}ye^{\mathrm{K}y}\right)\leq 0.
•
On \{\Gamma\leq 0\}, we have:
\partial^{2}_{yy}\Phi=\partial^{2}_{yy}A\Gamma+2\partial_{y}A\partial_{y}\Gamma-0.01\left(2\mathrm{K}e^{\mathrm{K}y}+\mathrm{K}^{2}e^{\mathrm{K}y}\right)=\mathrm{K}A\left(\mathrm{K}\Gamma+2\partial_{y}\Gamma\right)-0.01\left(2\mathrm{K}e^{\mathrm{K}y}+\mathrm{K}^{2}ye^{\mathrm{K}y}\right).
Here \Gamma\leq 0, and we know that \partial_{y}\Gamma\leq 0, so clearly \partial^{2}_{yy}\Phi\leq 0.
Since \Phi(\mathrm{K},\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}) is concave on [0,y_{\max}(\mathrm{K})], it is enough to prove that \Phi(\mathrm{K},y_{\max}(\mathrm{K}))\geq 0.
Step 4. Study at y=y_{\max}.
Plugging y=y_{\max}=\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}^{2}} into the expression of \Phi, we are left to show that:
3r_{\star}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}r_{\star}^{4}\mu_{\star}^{2}+3.01r_{\star}^{2}e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}}-\mathrm{K}r_{\star}^{2}}\min\left(0,\Gamma(\mathrm{K},y_{\max})\right)-3r_{\star}^{2}e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}}}-0.01\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}^{2}}e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}}}\geq 0.
with \Gamma(\mathrm{K},y_{\max}) given by:
\Gamma(\mathrm{K},y_{\max})=6+3\mathrm{K}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}-6\mathrm{K}\mu_{\star}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}+6r_{\star}^{2}\mu_{\star}^{2}-12\mathrm{K}r_{\star}^{2}.
Observe that:
•
The quantity e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}}-\mathrm{K}r_{\star}^{2}} is decreasing on [\mathrm{K}_{0},+\infty)
•
The quantity 3r_{\star}^{2}e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}}}+0.01\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}^{2}}e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}}} is decreasing on [\mathrm{K}_{0},+\infty)
•
The map \mathrm{K}\mapsto 6+3\mathrm{K}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}-6\mathrm{K}\mu_{\star}^{2}r_{\star}^{4}+6r_{\star}^{2}\mu_{\star}^{2}-12\mathrm{K}r_{\star}^{2} is bounded below by -3\left(2+2r_{\star}^{2}\mu_{\star}^{2}+r_{\star}^{4}\mu_{\star}^{4}\right).
It is thus enough to check that:
3r_{\star}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}r_{\star}^{4}\mu_{\star}^{2}-3.01r_{\star}^{2}e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}_{0}}-\mathrm{K}_{0}r_{\star}^{2}}\times 3\left(2+2r_{\star}^{2}\mu_{\star}^{2}+r_{\star}^{4}\mu_{\star}^{4}\right)-3r_{\star}^{2}e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}_{0}}}-0.01\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}_{0}^{2}}e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}_{0}}}\geq 0.
This is a purely numerical inequality which is true with our choices \bar{\alpha}=0.552 (and \mathrm{K}_{0}=\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}), \mu_{\star}=2.73.
∎
C.6 Third situation: |u| is “large”, and |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “small”.
This last regime is the most difficult one to study. The following lemma, whose proof occupies the next few pages, deals with the first shell.
Lemma C.5.
There exists a constant \mathtt{c}>0 such that the following holds. Assume that u,\alpha,v are such that:
|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\leq\sqrt{3.01}r_{\star}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\left(|u|^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)},\quad\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|\geq\mu_{\star}=2.73.
(C.23)
Then we have:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
Proof.
From (C.13), we know that:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}|(s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}-3r_{\star}^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(C.24)
Studying the full sum over the six vertices is challenging, but fortunately we can show that the contribution of a single “good” vertex of S^{\star} is sufficient to beat the negative term.
Choice of the good vertex.
Denote the vertex of S^{\star} in the direction of (1,0) by s_{1} and label the other vertices as shown on the picture below. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the angle \theta between s_{1} and the vector u is in [0,\frac{\pi}{6}], in which case we select s_{5} as our “good vertex”.
s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}s_{4}s_{5}s_{6}uv\theta
Figure 3: Without loss of generality, we assume that \theta\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{6}\right].
Focus on the contribution of s_{5}, expand the squares in the exponent, and write
|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s_{5}+u|^{2}}=|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s_{5}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
(C.25)
We want this to beat 3r_{\star}^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}. In that regard, the vertex s_{5} has two interesting features:
•
It is “opposite” to u, so the term -\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s_{5}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u in the exponent should be “very positive” (\alpha being “small”).
•
It is not aligned with u, so that (s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v should not be too small.
Indeed, the first condition in (C.23) tells us that |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “small”, thus u and v are “almost orthogonal”. If we chose the vertex s_{4}, which is “even more opposite” to u, there would be a risk to have (s_{4}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v\approx 0.
The rest of the proof of Lemma C.5 consists in showing that, with our conditions (C.23), we always have
|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s_{5}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}\geq 3r_{\star}^{2}+\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}.
(C.26)
Step 0. Admissible parameters.
•
Write u as u=(\rho\cos\theta,\rho\sin\theta). We have the following constraints:
\rho\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\text{ (because $u\in\mathcal{H}$)},\quad\theta\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{6}\right].
•
We recall that \alpha is such that
\alpha\leq\min\left(\bar{\alpha},\frac{\pi\rho}{\mu_{\star}}\right).
•
The vector v has norm 1 and must satisfy the condition
|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\leq b(\alpha):=\sqrt{3.01}r_{\star}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\left(|u|^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)}.
(C.27)
This condition is “increasing” in \alpha in the sense that for a fixed u, there are more admissible v’s when \alpha increases.
We consider the following function of u,\alpha,v:
\mathrm{F}(u,\alpha,v):=|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s_{5}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}.
(C.28)
Our goal is to prove that, for all admissible values of u,\alpha,v, we have:
\mathrm{F}(u,\alpha,v)\geq 3r_{\star}^{2}+\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}.
Step 1. Worst case for v.
We start by minimizing the prefactor |(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2} over v (there is no v-dependency in the exponential term).
Claim C.6.
Let u\in\mathbb{R}^{2} be a nonzero vector, let a\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, and \kappa\in[0,1]. Let z_{1}:=\frac{u}{|u|} and choose z_{2} such (z_{1},z_{2}) is an orthonormal basis of \mathbb{R}^{2}. Let a_{1},a_{2} be the coordinates of a in this basis. We have:
\min_{|v|=1,|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\leq\kappa|u|}|a\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|=\max\left(0,|a_{2}|\sqrt{1-\kappa^{2}}-|a_{1}|\kappa\right).
(C.29)
Proof.
Write v in the basis (z_{1},z_{2}) as v=(\cos\varphi,\sin\varphi) for some \varphi. We must then minimize the quantity \lvert a\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v\rvert=\lvert a_{1}\cos\varphi+a_{2}\sin\varphi\rvert under the constraint \lvert u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v\rvert\leq\kappa|u|, which is equivalent to \lvert\cos\varphi\rvert\leq\kappa.
For a fixed value of t:=\lvert\cos\varphi\rvert\in[0,\kappa], the quantity \lvert a_{1}\cos\varphi+a_{2}\sin\varphi\rvert is minimal when the two summands have opposite signs (so they subtract), in which case it is equal to \left||a_{2}|\sqrt{1-t^{2}}-|a_{1}|t\right|. Therefore:
\min_{|v|=1,|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\leq\kappa|u|}|a\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|=\min_{t\in[0,\kappa]}h(t),\qquad h(t):=\left||a_{2}|\sqrt{1-t^{2}}-|a_{1}|t\right|.
The function g:=t\mapsto|a_{2}|\sqrt{1-t^{2}}-|a_{1}|t is strictly decreasing on [0,1], with g(0)=\lvert a_{2}\rvert\geq 0, and g(\kappa)=\lvert a_{2}\rvert\sqrt{1-\kappa^{2}}-\lvert a_{1}\rvert\,\kappa. There are two cases:
•
If g(\kappa)\geq 0. Then g(t)\geq 0 for all t\in[0,\kappa], and h(t)=g(t)\geq g(\kappa) on [0,\kappa].
•
If g(\kappa)\leq 0. Since g(0)\geq 0 and g is continuous and strictly decreasing, there exists
t_{*}\in[0,\kappa] with g(t_{*})=0. Then h(t_{*})=\lvert g(t_{*})\rvert=0, and thus \min_{t\in[0,\kappa]}h(t)=0.
Combining both cases yields the result.
∎
In particular, choosing a=s_{5}+u, so that:
a_{1}=(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\frac{u}{|u|}=r_{\star}\cos\left(\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)+\rho=\rho-r_{\star}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right),\\
|a_{2}|=r_{\star}\left|\sin\left(\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\right|=r_{\star}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)
and letting \kappa=\kappa(\alpha,\rho), where
\kappa(\alpha,\rho):=\frac{b(\alpha)}{\rho},\text{ with }b(\alpha)=\sqrt{3.01}r_{\star}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\left(|u|^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)}\text{ as in \eqref{uvbalpha}},
applying (C.29) yields:
\mathrm{M}(u,\alpha):=\min_{|v|=1,|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\leq b(\alpha)}|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\\
=\max\left(0,r_{\star}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\alpha,\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left|\rho-r_{\star}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\right|\kappa(\alpha,\rho)\right),
(C.30)
and in particular we can write for all admissible u,\alpha,v:
\mathrm{F}(u,\alpha,v)\geq\mathrm{G}(u,\alpha):=\mathrm{M}(u,\alpha)^{2}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s_{5}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}.
(C.31)
Step 2. Worst case for \alpha.
Claim C.7.
For all admissible u,\alpha, we have:
\mathrm{G}(u,\alpha)\geq\mathrm{G}\left(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho)\right),\quad\alpha_{m}(\rho):=\min\left(\bar{\alpha},\ \frac{\pi\rho}{\mu_{\star}}\right).
(C.32)
Proof.
It follows from the fact that the map \alpha\mapsto\mathrm{G}(u,\alpha) is decreasing. Indeed:
•
Write s_{5}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u as -r_{\star}\rho\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right). Since \theta\in[0,\pi/6], we have \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\geq\tfrac{1}{2}, hence
2r_{\star}\rho\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)-\rho^{2}\geq r_{\star}\rho-\rho^{2}\geq 0,
(C.33)
because \rho\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}r_{\star}, thus the exponential term is decreasing in \alpha.
•
The quantity b(\alpha) defined in (C.27) is increasing in \alpha, hence the constraint |u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\leq b(\alpha) weakens as \alpha increases, and thus, for fixed u, the quantity \mathrm{M}(u,\alpha), defined as a minimum, is decreasing in \alpha.
The maximal admissible \alpha must satisfy both \alpha\leq\bar{\alpha} and \alpha\leq\frac{\pi\rho}{\mu_{\star}}, hence the expression (C.32) for \alpha_{m}.
∎
For u=(\rho\cos\theta,\rho\sin\theta), the quantity \mathrm{G}\left(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho)\right) is given, with \mathrm{M}(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho)) as in (C.30), by:
\mathrm{G}\left(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho)\right)=\mathrm{M}(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho))^{2}e^{\frac{2\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(2r_{\star}\rho\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)-\rho^{2}\right)}.
(C.34)
In the following, we will denote by \kappa(\rho) the quantity appearing in \mathrm{M}(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho)):
\kappa(\rho):=\kappa(\alpha_{m}(\rho),\rho):=\frac{b(\alpha_{m}(\rho))}{\rho}:=\sqrt{3.01}\frac{r_{\star}}{\rho}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(\rho^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)},\text{ with $\alpha_{m}(\rho):=\min\left(\bar{\alpha},\ \frac{\pi\rho}{\mu_{\star}}\right)$.}
(C.35)
Step 3. A quick study of \kappa.
With our choice for \mu_{\star}, the following holds.
Claim C.8.
The map \rho\mapsto\kappa(\rho) is increasing over \left[0,\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\right], and we have:
\max_{\rho\in\left[0,\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\right]}\kappa\left(\rho\right)=\kappa\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\sqrt{3.01}\times\sqrt{3}e^{-\frac{\pi}{3\bar{\alpha}}r_{\star}^{2}}\leq 0.337<\frac{1}{2}.
Proof.
In view of our expression for \alpha_{m}(\rho), define the threshold \rho_{0} as:
\rho_{0}:=\frac{\mu_{\star}\bar{\alpha}}{\pi},
(C.36)
so that if \rho\leq\rho_{0}, then \alpha_{m}(\rho)=\frac{\pi\rho}{\mu_{\star}} and if \rho\geq\rho_{0}, then \alpha_{m}(\rho)=\bar{\alpha}.
•
If \rho\leq\rho_{0}, the expression for \kappa(\rho) (see (C.35)) is \sqrt{3.01}\frac{r_{\star}}{\rho}e^{\frac{\mu_{\star}}{2}\left(\rho-\frac{r_{\star}^{2}}{\rho}\right)}. Positivity of its derivative is equivalent to \frac{\mu_{\star}}{2}\rho^{2}-\rho+\frac{\mu_{\star}}{2}r_{\star}^{2}\geq 0, which is true because the discriminant is negative, indeed:
\mu_{\star}\geq 1\geq\frac{1}{r_{\star}}.
•
If \rho\geq\rho_{0}, the expression for \kappa(\rho) is \sqrt{3.01}\frac{r_{\star}}{\rho}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\bar{\alpha}}\left(\rho^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)}. This is increasing if \rho\geq\sqrt{\frac{\bar{\alpha}}{\pi}}, but here \rho\geq\rho_{0}=\frac{\mu_{\star}\bar{\alpha}}{\pi} and we do have \mu_{\star}\geq\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}}.
This shows that \rho\mapsto\kappa(\rho) is increasing. Finally, we simply compute
\kappa\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\sqrt{3.01}\times\sqrt{3}e^{-\frac{\pi}{3\bar{\alpha}}r_{\star}^{2}}\leq 0.337<\frac{1}{2}.
∎
It will be relevant in the sequel to notice that, with our choice for \mu_{\star}, we have:
\rho_{0}=\frac{\mu_{\star}\bar{\alpha}}{\pi}\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{2}.
Step 4. Checking the positivity of the prefactor.
Claim C.9.
The quantity r_{\star}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left|\rho-r_{\star}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\right|\kappa(\rho) is always positive.
Proof.
Since \theta\in[0,\pi/6], we have \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}, as well as 0\leq\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\leq\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, which implies:
\left|\rho-r_{\star}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\right|\leq\max\left(\rho,r_{\star}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\right)\leq\max\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}.
It is thus enough to show that \left(\sqrt{1-\kappa(\rho)^{2}}-\sqrt{3}\kappa(\rho)\right)\geq 0 for all admissible \rho. This is equivalent to having \kappa(\rho)\leq\frac{1}{2}, which we know is true.
∎
As a consequence, the prefactor \mathrm{M}(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho)) in (C.34) is always given, cf. (C.30), by
\mathrm{M}(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho))=r_{\star}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left|\rho-r_{\star}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\right)\right|\kappa(\rho).
(C.37)
Step 5. Re-expressing \mathrm{G}\left(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho)\right)
Introduce the following additional variables:
\phi:=\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\in\left[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}\right],\quad\delta(\rho):=\arcsin\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)
In view of (C.37) we can write, using the variable \phi:
\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi):=\mathrm{M}(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho))=r_{\star}\sin\left(\phi\right)\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left|\rho-r_{\star}\cos\left(\phi\right)\right|\kappa(\rho),
(C.38)
the only ambiguity being the sign of \rho-r_{\star}\cos\left(\phi\right). There are several cases:
•
If \rho\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{2}, then for all \phi\in\left[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}\right] we have
\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)=r_{\star}\sin\left(\phi\right)\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-r_{\star}\cos\left(\phi\right)\kappa(\rho)+\rho\kappa(\rho)=r_{\star}\sin(\phi-\delta(\rho))+\rho\kappa(\rho).
(C.39)
•
If \rho\geq\frac{r_{\star}}{2} and \frac{\pi}{6}\leq\phi\leq\arccos\left(\frac{\rho}{r_{\star}}\right), we have again:
\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)=r_{\star}\sin(\phi-\delta(\rho))+\rho\kappa(\rho).
•
If \rho\geq\frac{r_{\star}}{2} and \arccos\left(\frac{\rho}{r_{\star}}\right)\leq\phi\leq\frac{\pi}{3}, we have instead:
\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)=r_{\star}\sin\left(\phi\right)\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}+r_{\star}\cos\left(\phi\right)\kappa(\rho)-\rho\kappa(\rho)=r_{\star}\sin(\phi+\delta(\rho))-\rho\kappa(\rho).
We are left to study the following map over [0,\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}]\times[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}], cf. (C.34)
\mathrm{H}:(\rho,\phi)\mapsto\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)^{2}\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(2r_{\star}\rho\cos\phi-\rho^{2}\right)\right).
Step 5. Worst case for \phi.
Claim C.10.
For all admissible \rho, the quantity \mathrm{H}(\rho,\phi) is minimal at \phi=\frac{\pi}{3}.
Proof.
The proof goes in two steps: first, we show that the minimum is always at \frac{\pi}{3} or \frac{\pi}{6}, then we compare the two values directly and find that the smaller one is always at \frac{\pi}{3}.
1. The minimum is at the endpoints. It suffices to show that \partial_{\phi}\mathrm{H}(\rho,\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}) is decreasing for fixed \rho. Write:
\partial_{\phi}\mathrm{H}(\rho,\phi)=\left(2\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)\partial_{\phi}\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)-\frac{2\pi r_{\star}\rho}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)^{2}\sin\phi\right)\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(2r_{\star}\rho\cos\phi-\rho^{2}\right)\right),
and recall that \mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi) is always positive, thus the sign of \partial_{\phi}\mathrm{H}(\rho,\phi) is the same as the sign of
\mathrm{T}(\rho,\phi):=\partial_{\phi}\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)-\frac{\pi r_{\star}\rho}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)\sin\phi.
We split the discussion into several cases.
•
If \rho\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{2}, we know from (C.39) that
\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)=r_{\star}\sin(\phi-\delta)+\rho\kappa(\rho),\text{ and thus }\partial_{\phi}\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)=r_{\star}\cos(\phi-\delta),
in which case we obtain the following expression for \mathrm{T}(\rho,\phi):
\mathrm{T}(\rho,\phi)=r_{\star}\cos(\phi-\delta)-\frac{\pi r_{\star}\rho}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(r_{\star}\sin(\phi-\delta)+\rho\kappa(\rho)\right)\sin\phi.
(C.40)
Since 0\leq\delta\leq\frac{\pi}{6}, this is strictly decreasing for \phi\in[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}].
•
If \rho\geq\frac{r_{\star}}{2}, the expression for \mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi) changes when \phi reaches \arccos\left(\frac{\rho}{r_{\star}}\right), so we distinguish two intervals:
–
On \left[\frac{\pi}{6},\arccos\left(\frac{\rho}{r_{\star}}\right)\right], the expression for \mathrm{T}(\rho,\phi) is as above, and still strictly decreasing in \phi.
–
On \left[\arccos\left(\frac{\rho}{r_{\star}}\right),\frac{\pi}{3}\right], we have instead:
\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)=r_{\star}\sin(\phi+\delta)-\rho\kappa(\rho),\text{ and thus }\partial_{\phi}\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)=r_{\star}\cos(\phi+\delta),
which yields the following expression for \mathrm{T}(\rho,\phi)
\mathrm{T}(\rho,\phi)=r_{\star}\cos(\phi+\delta)-\frac{\pi r_{\star}\rho}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(r_{\star}\sin(\phi+\delta)-\rho\kappa(\rho)\right)\sin\phi,
which is again strictly decreasing in \phi.
2. The minimum is at \frac{\pi}{3}. We now compare the values of \mathrm{H}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6}) and \mathrm{H}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3}) in different regimes, and show that:
\frac{\mathrm{H}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{H}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})}\right)^{2}\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}r_{\star}\rho\left(\sqrt{3}-1\right)\right)\geq 1.
(C.41)
First, observe that since we assume \frac{\pi}{\alpha}\rho\geq\mu_{\star}, we have:
\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}r_{\star}\rho\left(\sqrt{3}-1\right)\right)\geq\exp\left(\mu_{\star}r_{\star}\left(\sqrt{3}-1\right)\right)\approx 8.56
and we are left to prove that the ratio \frac{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})} cannot be too small, so that:
\left(\frac{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})}\right)^{2}\exp\left(\mu_{\star}r_{\star}\left(\sqrt{3}-1\right)\right)\geq 1.
•
If 0\leq\rho\leq\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}. Then of course \rho\leq\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}. According to the expressions for \mathrm{N} given in (C.38), we have:
\mathrm{N}\left(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}-\rho\right)\kappa(\rho),\quad\mathrm{N}\left(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left(\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\rho\right)\kappa(\rho).
For \bar{\kappa}=\kappa(\rho) fixed, a quick computation shows that the map
\tilde{\rho}\mapsto\frac{\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\bar{\kappa}^{2}}-\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}-\tilde{\rho}\right)\bar{\kappa}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\bar{\kappa}^{2}}-\left(\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\tilde{\rho}\right)\bar{\kappa}}=\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\bar{\kappa}^{2}}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\bar{\kappa}\right)+\tilde{\rho}\bar{\kappa}}{\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\bar{\kappa}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}\bar{\kappa}\right)+\tilde{\rho}\bar{\kappa}}
is increasing, and thus minimal at 0. We obtain:
\frac{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})}\geq\frac{\sqrt{1-\bar{\kappa}^{2}}-\sqrt{3}\bar{\kappa}}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{1-\bar{\kappa}^{2}}-\bar{\kappa}},
and this quantity is decreasing in \bar{\kappa}. Since \rho\mapsto\kappa(\rho) is increasing, we have \bar{\kappa}\leq\kappa\left(\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\right), and thus:
\frac{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})}\geq\frac{\sqrt{1-\kappa\left(\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\right)^{2}}-\sqrt{3}\kappa\left(\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\right)}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{1-\kappa\left(\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\right)^{2}}-\kappa\left(\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\right)}.
To prove (C.41), it remains to check the purely numerical inequality:
\left(\frac{\sqrt{1-\kappa\left(\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\right)^{2}}-\sqrt{3}\kappa\left(\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\right)}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{1-\kappa\left(\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\right)^{2}}-\kappa\left(\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\right)}\right)^{2}\exp\left(\mu_{\star}r_{\star}\left(\sqrt{3}-1\right)\right)\geq 1.
•
If \frac{9r_{\star}}{20}\leq\rho\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}r_{\star}. Now, we write:
\mathrm{N}\left(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{9}{20}\right)r_{\star}\kappa(\rho),
and observe that even if the expression of \mathrm{N}\left(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3}\right) changes at \rho=\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}, we always have:
\mathrm{N}\left(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\leq\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}.
Dividing each term by \frac{1}{2}r_{\star} gives the lower bound:
\frac{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})}\geq\frac{\sqrt{1-\kappa^{2}}-\left(\sqrt{3}-\frac{9}{10}\right)\kappa}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{1-\kappa^{2}}}.
(C.42)
This quantity is decreasing in \kappa and thus (since \kappa is increasing with \rho)
\frac{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})}\geq\frac{\sqrt{1-\kappa\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}r_{\star}\right)^{2}}-\left(\sqrt{3}-\frac{9}{10}\right)\kappa\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}r_{\star}\right)}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{1-\kappa\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}r_{\star}\right)^{2}}}.
To prove (C.41), it remains to check the purely numerical inequality:
\left(\frac{\sqrt{1-\kappa\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}r_{\star}\right)^{2}}-\left(\sqrt{3}-\frac{9}{10}\right)\kappa\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}r_{\star}\right)}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{1-\kappa\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}r_{\star}\right)^{2}}}\right)^{2}\exp\left(\mu_{\star}r_{\star}\left(\sqrt{3}-1\right)\right)\geq 1.
∎
As a consequence, for all admissible values of \rho, letting
\widetilde{\mathrm{N}}(\rho):=\mathrm{N}\left(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left|\rho-\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}\right|\kappa(\rho),
we obtain the following lower bound on \mathrm{H}(\rho,\phi):
\mathrm{H}(\rho,\phi)\geq\mathrm{I}(\rho):=\mathrm{H}\left(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\widetilde{\mathrm{N}}(\rho)^{2}\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(r_{\star}\rho-\rho^{2}\right)\right).
Step 6. Worst case for \rho.
Claim C.11.
For all admissible \rho, we have \mathrm{I}(\rho)\geq\mathrm{I}\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\right).
Proof.
We consider three possibilities for \rho: between 0 and \rho_{0}, between \rho_{0} and \frac{1}{2}r_{\star}, between \frac{1}{2}r_{\star} and \frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}.
•
If 0\leq\rho\leq\rho_{0}\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{2}, we have:
\widetilde{\mathrm{N}}(\rho)=\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left(\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\rho\right)\kappa(\rho)\right),\quad\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(r_{\star}\rho-\rho^{2}\right)\right)=\exp\left(\mu_{\star}\left(r_{\star}-\rho\right)\right),
and thus the sign of \mathrm{I}^{\prime}(\rho) is the same as the sign of 2\widetilde{\mathrm{N}}^{\prime}(\rho)-\mu_{\star}\widetilde{\mathrm{N}}(\rho). We claim that \mathrm{I}^{\prime}(\rho)\leq 0. Indeed:
–
We know by Claim C.8 that \rho\mapsto\kappa(\rho) is increasing and thus:
\rho\mapsto\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}\text{ is decreasing,}\quad-\left(\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\rho\right)\kappa^{\prime}(\rho)\text{ is negative,}
in particular we see that \widetilde{\mathrm{N}}^{\prime}(\rho)\leq\kappa(\rho).
–
We have \widetilde{\mathrm{N}}\geq\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}\kappa(\rho)
It remains to check that for all 0\leq\kappa\leq\kappa\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\right) we have:
2\kappa-\mu_{\star}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\kappa^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}\kappa\right)\leq 0,
which boils down to a quadratic inequality in \kappa that can be checked by hand.
•
If \rho_{0}\leq\rho\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{2}, the expression of \widetilde{\mathrm{N}}(\rho) does not change but \exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(r_{\star}\rho-\rho^{2}\right)\right)=\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}\left(r_{\star}\rho-\rho^{2}\right)\right). Since \rho\leq\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}, this exponential term is increasing. We claim that \widetilde{\mathrm{N}}(\rho) is also increasing, which will prove that \mathrm{I}(\rho) is increasing on this interval. We write:
\widetilde{\mathrm{N}}^{\prime}(\rho)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\frac{-\kappa(\rho)\kappa^{\prime}(\rho)}{\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}}+\kappa-\left(\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\rho\right)\kappa^{\prime}(\rho)=\kappa(\rho)-\kappa^{\prime}(\rho)\left(\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\rho+\frac{\sqrt{3}r_{\star}\kappa(\rho)}{2\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}}\right).
Since \rho\geq\rho_{0}, we have \alpha_{m}(\rho)=\bar{\alpha} and \kappa(\rho) is given, see (C.35), by:
\kappa(\rho)=\left(\sqrt{3.01}r_{\star}e^{-\frac{\pi}{2\bar{\alpha}}r_{\star}^{2}}\right)\times\frac{1}{\rho}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\bar{\alpha}}\rho^{2}},\quad\kappa^{\prime}(\rho)=\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}\rho^{2}-1\right)\kappa(\rho).
After factoring out \kappa(\rho), which is positive, we are left to show that:
1-\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}\rho^{2}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\rho+\frac{\sqrt{3}r_{\star}\kappa(\rho)}{2\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}}\right)\geq 0.
We now use some simple bounds: \frac{1}{\rho}\leq\frac{1}{\rho_{0}}, \frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}\rho^{2}\leq\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{2}\right)^{2}, \frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\rho\leq\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\rho_{0}, \frac{\kappa(\rho)}{\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}}\leq\frac{\kappa\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{2}\right)\right)^{2}}} (because \kappa is increasing), and we obtain the purely numerical inequality:
1-\frac{1}{\rho_{0}}\left(\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{2}\right)^{2}-1\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}-\rho_{0}+\frac{\sqrt{3}r_{\star}}{2}\frac{\kappa\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{2}\right)\right)^{2}}}\right)\geq 0,
which is true.
•
If \frac{r_{\star}}{2}\leq\rho\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}, we have:
\widetilde{\mathrm{N}}(\rho)=\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}r_{\star}\sqrt{1-\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)^{2}}-\left(\rho-\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}\right)\kappa(\rho)\right),\quad\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(r_{\star}\rho-\rho^{2}\right)\right)=\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}\left(r_{\star}\rho-\rho^{2}\right)\right).
Since \rho\geq\frac{r_{\star}}{2}, we have \left(r_{\star}\rho-\rho^{2}\right)^{\prime}\leq 0, so the exponential term is decreasing. On the other hand \widetilde{\mathrm{N}} is also decreasing, because \kappa increases.
From this study, we get that \mathrm{I} is decreasing on [0,\rho_{0}], then increasing on [\rho_{0},\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}], and then decreasing again on [\frac{1}{2}r_{\star},\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}].
Numerically, one finds
\mathrm{I}(\rho_{0})>\mathrm{I}\left(\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\approx 3.581\text{ versus }3r_{\star}^{2}\approx 3.464.
∎
Step 7. Conclusion.
Returning to (C.28), we have found that for all admissible u,\alpha,v, we have:
|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s_{5}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}\geq 3r_{\star}^{2}+0.1
In view of (C.24), (C.25), we can then guarantee that:
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq 0.1e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.
Since u\in\mathcal{H} is bounded, we may write |u|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{c}0.1 for \mathtt{c} small enough, and we obtain (C.13).
∎
C.7 Higher shells
We conclude this section with a quick study of higher shells. We claim that if S is shell of radius r\geq r_{\star\star}:=r_{\star}\sqrt{3} (the second smallest non-zero distance between lattice points), we have:
\sum_{s\in S}|(s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}-3r^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r^{2}}\geq 0.
(C.43)
We also split the discussion into two cases, which are easier to treat than their “first shell” counterparts.
Lemma C.12 (\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u| small).
Assume that u,\alpha are such that:
\alpha\leq\bar{\alpha},\quad\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|\leq\hat{\mu}:=1.5.
(C.44)
Then (C.43) holds.
Proof.
We follow the same strategy of proof as for Lemma C.4: perform a Taylor expansion to third order and use the symmetries of the hexagon. Replacing r_{\star} by r in (C.19), (C.20), (C.22), we obtain that (C.43) holds if:
3r^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{K}^{2}r^{4}|u|^{2}+|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\left(6+3\mathrm{K}^{2}r^{4}\left(1-2\mathrm{K}|u|^{2}\right)+6\mathrm{K}r^{2}\left(\mathrm{K}|u|^{2}-2\right)\right)\geq 3r^{2}e^{\mathrm{K}|u|^{2}}.
We still have the constraints \mathrm{K}\geq\mathrm{K}_{0}:=\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}, and \mu:=\mathrm{K}|u|\leq\hat{\mu}. The good news is that the quantity within the parenthesis is now non-negative: write it as
6+3\mathrm{K}^{2}r^{4}-6\mathrm{K}r^{4}\mu^{2}+6\mu^{2}r^{2}-12\mathrm{K}r^{2}\geq 6+3\mathrm{K}^{2}r^{4}-6\mathrm{K}r^{4}\hat{\mu}^{2}+6\hat{\mu}^{2}r^{2}-12\mathrm{K}r^{2}
the critical point of this convex quantity \mathrm{K}=\hat{\mu}^{2}+\frac{2}{r^{2}}\leq\mathrm{K}_{0}, so the minimal value is at \mathrm{K}_{0}, furthermore:
\frac{\mathtt{d}}{\mathtt{d}r}\left(6+3\mathrm{K}_{0}^{2}r^{4}-6\mathrm{K}_{0}r^{4}\hat{\mu}^{2}+6\hat{\mu}^{2}r^{2}-12\mathrm{K}_{0}r^{2}\right)\geq 0\iff r^{2}\geq\frac{2\mathrm{K}_{0}-\hat{\mu}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}_{0}^{2}-2\mathrm{K}_{0}\hat{\mu}^{2}},
which is true for r\geq r_{\star\star}:=\sqrt{3}r_{\star}, and we can finally check a purely numerical inequality:
6+3\mathrm{K}_{0}^{2}r^{4}-6\mathrm{K}_{0}r^{4}\hat{\mu}^{2}+6\hat{\mu}^{2}r^{2}-12\mathrm{K}_{0}r^{2}\geq 6+3\mathrm{K}_{0}^{2}r_{\star\star}^{4}-6\mathrm{K}_{0}r_{\star\star}^{4}\hat{\mu}^{2}+6\hat{\mu}^{2}r_{\star\star}^{2}-12\mathrm{K}_{0}r_{\star\star}^{2}\geq 0.
We are thus left to prove that, for all admissible \mathrm{K},u,
1+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{K}^{2}r^{2}|u|^{2}\geq e^{\mathrm{K}|u|^{2}},\text{ i.e. }1+\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}r^{2}\geq e^{\frac{\mu^{2}}{\mathrm{K}}}
which again boils down to an explicit computation: the worst case for \mathrm{K} is at \mathrm{K}=\mathrm{K}_{0}, and the quantity 1+\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}r^{2}-e^{\frac{\mu^{2}}{\mathrm{K}_{0}}} is concave in \mu^{2}, vanishes at \mu^{2}=0, so it remains to check that:
1+\frac{1}{2}\hat{\mu}^{2}r^{2}-e^{\frac{\hat{\mu}^{2}}{\mathrm{K}_{0}}}\geq 0,
which is true with our choices \bar{\alpha}=0.552 (and \mathrm{K}_{0}=\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}), \hat{\mu}=1.5.
∎
Lemma C.13 (\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u| large).
Assume that u,\alpha are such that:
\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|\geq\hat{\mu}:=1.5
Then (C.43) holds.
Proof.
We follow a similar strategy as for the proof of Lemma C.5. Returning to the situation shown in Figure 3, we now focus on the contributions of s_{5} and s_{4} together. The first key observation is that, taking \theta\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{6}\right] as in Figure 3, we have both \pi-\theta and \pi+\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta in \left[\pi-\frac{\pi}{3},\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}\right], hence:
s_{4}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\leq-\frac{1}{2}r|u|,\quad s_{5}\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u\leq-\frac{1}{2}r|u|.
The contributions from s_{4} and s_{5} are thus bounded below by:
|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s_{5}+u|^{2}}+|(s_{4}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s_{4}+u|^{2}}\geq\left(|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}+|(s_{4}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\right)e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r^{2}-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}+\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r|u|},
and to get (C.43) it suffices to prove:
\left(|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}+|(s_{4}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\right)e^{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}\left(r|u|-|u|^{2}\right)}\geq 3r^{2}.
(C.45)
Claim C.14.
We have
|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}+|(s_{4}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\geq r^{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3|u|^{2}}{r^{2}}\right)
Proof.
Write v=(\cos\phi,\sin\phi). Expanding the squares, using that (s_{5}+s_{4})\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v=\sqrt{3}r\cos\left(\pi+\frac{\pi}{6}-\phi\right) (see Figure 3), and that (u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)\geq-|u|, we get:
|(s_{5}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}+|(s_{4}+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}=r^{2}\left(\cos^{2}(\pi-\phi)+\cos^{2}(\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}-\phi)\right)+2\left((s_{5}+s_{4})\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v\right)(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)+2|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\\
\geq r^{2}\left(\cos^{2}(\phi)+\cos^{2}\left(\phi-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)-2\sqrt{3}|u|r\left|\cos\left(\phi-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right|=r^{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\cos^{2}\left(\phi-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)-2\sqrt{3}|u|r\left|\cos\left(\phi-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right|.
The minimum of c\mapsto r^{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}+c^{2}\right)-2\sqrt{3}|u|rc for c\in[0,1] is \frac{r^{2}}{2}-3|u|^{2}.
∎
In order to get (C.45), it remains to show that:
\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3|u|^{2}}{r^{2}}\right)e^{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}\left(r|u|-|u|^{2}\right)}\geq 3.
The worst possibility for r is the smallest one, namely r=r_{\star\star}:=\sqrt{3}r_{\star}. Let
\mathrm{F}(\alpha,\rho):=\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\rho^{2}}{r_{\star}^{2}}\right)e^{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}\left(\sqrt{3}r_{\star}\rho-\rho^{2}\right)}.
A direct computation shows that for fixed \alpha, \log\mathrm{F}(\alpha,\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}) is strictly concave in \rho and thus attains its minimum at the endpoints of the admissible interval defined by the conditions \frac{\pi}{\alpha}\rho\geq\hat{\mu} and \rho\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}, i.e. at \rho=\frac{\hat{\mu}\alpha}{\pi} or at \rho=\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}. With our choices of \bar{\alpha}=0.552,\hat{\mu}=1.5, we have on the one hand:
\mathrm{F}\left(\alpha,\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\geq\mathrm{F}\left(\bar{\alpha},\frac{r_{\star}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{1}{6}e^{\frac{\pi}{\bar{\alpha}}\frac{4}{3\sqrt{3}}}>3,
and on the other hand:
\mathrm{F}\left(\alpha,\frac{\hat{\mu}\alpha}{\pi}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\hat{\mu}^{2}\alpha^{2}}{\pi^{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\right)e^{\sqrt{3}r_{\star}\hat{\mu}-\frac{\hat{\mu}^{2}\alpha}{\pi}}\geq\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\hat{\mu}^{2}\bar{\alpha}^{2}}{\pi^{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\right)e^{\sqrt{3}r_{\star}\hat{\mu}-\frac{\hat{\mu}^{2}\bar{\alpha}}{\pi}}>3.
∎
Table 1: Table of Notations and Constants
\mathsf{A}_{2}
The hexagonal lattice (of density 1).
\mathcal{H}
Fundamental domain (Voronoi cell) of \mathsf{A}_{2}.
\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}
The reciprocal lattice of \mathsf{A}_{2}.
\Omega
Fundamental domain of \widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} (Pontryagin dual).
S^{\star}
The first shell (6 nearest neighbors) of \mathsf{A}_{2}.
r_{\star}
Minimal distance of \mathsf{A}_{2}, \sqrt{2/\sqrt{3}}.
r_{\star\star}
The second smallest non-zero distance, r_{\star}\sqrt{3}.
c.m.s.d.
Completely monotonic function of square distance.
\Phi_{\alpha}
Gaussian potential, r\mapsto e^{-\pi\alpha r^{2}}.
\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)
Gaussian function on \mathbb{R}^{2}, \mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)=\Phi_{\alpha}(|x|).
\mathrm{W}_{f}
Bernstein measure for a c.m.s.d. function f.
\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{X})
The f-energy per point of \mathsf{X}.
\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{X})
The \Phi_{\alpha}-energy of \mathsf{X}.
\mathbf{p}
A perturbation map \mathbf{p}:\mathsf{A}_{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}.
\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}
The perturbed lattice configuration.
\|\mathbf{p}\|
Size of the perturbation, \sup_{x}|\mathbf{p}(x)|.
\mathrm{Q}_{x}
Probability measure of relative displacements.
\mathrm{C}_{x}
Covariance matrix of relative displacements.
\mathrm{R}_{x}
Autocorrelation matrix of the perturbation field.
\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p})
First-Shell size of \mathbf{p}, \sum_{x\in S^{\star}}\int|u|^{2}d\mathrm{Q}_{x}.
\widehat{\mathsf{R}}
The \mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}-valued spectral measure of \mathbf{p}.
\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}
The trace measure \widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{11}+\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{22}.
\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}
The trace derivative, d\widehat{\mathsf{R}}/d\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}.
\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p})
Spectral Measure size of \mathbf{p}, \mathtt{tr}(\int|\omega|^{2}d\widehat{\mathsf{R}}).
\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)
Auxiliary lattice sum \sum|(x+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|x+u|^{2}}.
\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)
Contribution to \Psi_{\alpha,v}(u) from S^{\star}\cup\{0\}.
\alpha_{\dagger}
Threshold \alpha separating large/small regimes.
\bar{\alpha}
Numerical constant, 0.552.
\mu_{\star}
Numerical constant, 2.73.
\hat{\mu}
Numerical constant, 1.5.
